# DssHarness architecture

## Why this exists

A repository's build, test and cross-host work is usually a pile of paired
`.sh`/`.ps1` scripts that drift apart, encode one repository's facts, and fail
differently on each platform. `DssHarness` replaces that with one
cross-platform .NET tool whose behaviour is driven entirely by `config.json`.

**Nothing about any specific repository, language or toolchain is compiled in.**
If a behaviour cannot be expressed in `config.json`, that is a defect.

## Status

Implemented today: `init`, `verify-git`, `create-worktree`, `delete-worktree`,
`list-worktree`, the orchestrator commands (`create-orchestrator`, `delete-orchestrator`,
`list-orchestrator`, `create-agent`, `seed-agent`, `refresh-agent`, `rebase-agent`,
`fold-agent`, `delete-agent`), the run commands (`run-orchestrator`, `resume-orchestrator`,
`answer-orchestrator`, `amend-orchestrator-request`, `pause-orchestrator`, `stop-orchestrator`, `ask-orchestrator-status`, `ask-orchestrator`, `read-orchestrator-report`, `analyze-orchestrator-report`; the steps `FlowStepRunners.Served` lists are served - `orient`, `graphify-codebase`, `validate-plan`, `create-agent`, `reason`, `build`, `test`, `run`, `check-mutations`, `anchor-balance`, `anchor-citations`, `class-closure`, `route-findings`, `ci-read`, `ci-wait`, `fold`, `delete-agent`, `refresh`, `rebase`, `commit`, `push`, `pull-request` - and a step of any other type fails until its runner lands), the side-task commands (`run-side-task`, `list-side-tasks`), `validate-workflow`, `export-workflow`, `list-agent-providers`, `check-root-litter`, the anchor commands (`write-anchor`, `set-anchor`,
`read-anchor`, `read-anchors`, `check-anchor-balance`, `check-anchor-arms`, `check-anchor-citations`),
`fix-line-endings`, `check-ci-legs`, `legs`, `host-exec`, `install-missing-tools`,
`update-tool`, `sync`, `build`, `test`, `run`, `check-mutations`, `stop-run`, `query-codebase-graph`, `clean`, `up`,
`down`, `queue` and `help`.

Every section of this document now describes code that exists. Where a rule is stated in
the present tense it is enforced, and a gap between the two is a defect in the tool rather
than a section still waiting to be written.

## Layering

```
DssHarness.Cli        Program.cs and Commands/: argument parsing, the console and the exit code only
DssHarness.Core       domain, services, abstractions; the lifecycle every command shares
                      (Application), the registrations (Composition) and the help's text (Help)
dss-harness-test      tests

(DssHarness.Adapters was planned for the build adapters; they arrived in
DssHarness.Core instead, beside the build service that is their only caller, and the
project was not created.)
```

`Core` is a library, so "no logic in Program.cs" is enforced by the assembly
boundary rather than by discipline. The seam a front end reaches Core through is narrower
still, and held by tests rather than discipline (`ArchitectureTests`, which read the
command line's own assembly metadata): every Core type the command line references is in
the application layer (`Application\`: the use cases, their requests and results, the
session and pipeline every command shares), its help (`Help\`), its output (`Output\`) or
its results (`Results\`); or is reached from an operation of a use case - a request, a
result, and everything they are made of: their properties and fields, their bases, and the
elements and arguments of their collections and generics, never a static helper beside a use
case or a method of what it hands over - computed from the assemblies themselves and never
listed by hand; or is one of a few reviewed types, each with its reason on the list: a name
Core's own sentences or wire say (a command's name, an option's, a cell's), the console's
own pieces (a password prompt, a side-task's terminal, a run session's counted
interrupts), the renderers of the reports the use cases answer, the composition root every
front end calls once, and the hidden process commands the program runs for itself. A
reviewed entry nothing references any more, or one a use case reaches, is taken off the
list - the test demands both. None of the platform's seams (`IFileSystem`, `IProcessRunner`,
`IGitClient`, `IHostPlatform`, `IHarnessContextLoader`) is ever among them, so a front end
never reads a file or runs a program itself: a `--<cell>-file` is read by the anchors' use
case. The services a command only calls are marked as the use cases
they are (`: IUseCase`) where they live, from verify-git's to the checks', so their requests
and their reports are contracts a front end may read. A service only the engine calls is
none: `IAgentRunner`, whose request carries what the engine built for a step out of the
machine's seams - the codebase graph's tool among it - is reached by a front end only through
the use cases that drive an agent, an orchestrator's run and a side-task. Nothing in Core outside
`Application\`, `Composition\` and `Help\` reaches into them: the layer below shares the
layer's contracts but never its machinery - its sessions, its scopes, its document kinds,
its pipeline. That is read from the core's own metadata, not its source's text: every type a
type below the layers names in its signatures, its locals and its bodies' instructions, however
its source spells it. The layer's contracts are its use cases with their requests and results,
and the few points it is open to below it, each reviewed with its reason - the facts every
document of an operation says (`IDocumentFacts`), which the service that did them fills, and
what an operation writes at its end once its work has stopped (`IEndWrites`), which the service
that writes it answers and a terminal's second interrupt says is still to come. The
one scan of the core for a contract's implementations (`CoreImplementations<T>`) is the
core's own, at its root, so the registries below the layer that read it never reach into the
composition root that registers what it finds. The command line builds no container: the registrations are the core's own
(`ServiceRegistration.AddDssHarness`), so a front end other than the command line builds the
same services; the core builds each operation's provider (`ServiceRegistration.Host`), and
the command line supplies only how a password is asked at its terminal (`ConsoleHost`). And
no command's wiring outgrows 220 lines but the two files that declare several commands'
options, so a file under `Commands\` is wiring, and wiring is all a person reads in it.

### What every area shares: pages, walks, waits and text

Four folders of Core sit above the file system, the output and the platform seam and below every area that answers,
walks or waits - the agents, the codebase graph, the engine, the web, git and CI, runs, sync, hosts, execution,
mutations and anchors - and each holds one rule those areas ask of it, so no area answers a large input, a deep one or a
slow one by a number of its own. They reach files only through `IFileSystem`, time only through `TimeProvider` and a
process's life only through `IProcessIdentity`; they tell what they wait on through a callback, never through the
console or `IHarnessOutput`; and nothing in them branches on the operating system - a thread given a stack of a size is
.NET's own on every system.

- `Pages\`: an answer's pages. No answer is cut: each is pages of whole entries, page 1 given and any page asked by
  number, its totals counted exactly (`Paging`, over each answer's own entry, `IPageEntry`); an entry wider than a page
  is given in pieces at character boundaries, each marked where it goes on, by one rule (`Pieces`); and how much a page
  holds has one owner (`PageRoom`) - a page's size, never a limit, since every entry stays reachable. A conversation's
  kept answers are `KeptAnswers`: one file an ask in the conversation's directory, read once and then held, every one
  kept for the conversation's life and put away when it ends, the work it goes on from read nearest first, and an
  answer kept under another state - the graph moved, the file changed - never given for this one (`IKeptFreshness`). A
  text file's pages (`TextPages`) are laid by streaming the file once and keep only the byte offsets where pages begin;
  a page is read by seeking to its own, so a two-gigabyte log costs a page's memory. A text laid with the blocks its
  writer kept beside it (`TextBlocks`: each block's head, the lines after it and its end by the bytes the file holds them
  at, read a line at a time in the same pass, then the digest of the bytes they were written beside) gives a page that
  begins inside a block the block's head again first, its mark naming where the file holds the head
  (`TextPageMark.Head`), said as going on and counting nothing, by the one rule a page laid in memory gives a result's
  block's head again by (`Paging.HoldsAgain`: only where the room left beside it holds the least piece of what follows,
  `Pieces.Least`, so no page passes its room); blocks that are not the text's - another schema's, out of order, past its
  end, or written beside bytes it no longer holds - give it none, and its pages are laid as its lines alone.
- `Walks\`: a walk on an explicit stack or queue that keeps a set of what it met (`Walk`); a memo that answers each key
  once from its dependencies' answers, and a key met again while it is being answered by the cycle's own rule (`Memo`);
  answers made once where making one asks for others as it is made, through any store sharing its makings, a memo
  given them among them (`MadeOnce`, `Makings`), the makings taken as the graph they make and its strongly connected sets
  found as they close, on the making stack alone and with no recursion: a key asked again while it is being made -
  directly or through any store that shares the makings - is a cycle; every key of a strongly connected set of makings
  that holds a cycle answers its placeholder, nothing known, with whatever its store keeps beside it of what the whole set
  read, and every read of such a key, while the set is made and after, is given that answer; every other key keeps the
  answer its making made; each key is made once, each set is closed once as its outermost making ends, and nothing kept
  is ever made again - so the answer a key keeps does not depend on which key of it is asked first, and the work is
  linear in the makings and the reads, however deep the cycles nest;
  a chain followed to its end or its first revisit (`Chain`); a step repeated until it says it is done or its state
  repeats, which is told as a cycle (`Fixpoint`); and a recursion moved onto a thread of a larger stack where the stack
  runs short - our own at each level (`DeepCalls.Run`), a library's we do not own on a thread whose stack holds the depth
  it was measured to need (`DeepCalls.RunSized`). A walk is linear in what is true, cycles included, and no depth, count
  or visit budget ends one; a .NET thread's stack is an `int` count of bytes, the runtime's fact, and a depth past it is
  refused naming it.
- `Waiting\`: a wait for the thing itself - a work's end, a lock's holder ending (`Waits`) - told every five minutes
  (`Waits.SaidEvery`, the cadence an admission's wait keeps), cancellable, and ended only at the bound the user
  configured; and the one owner of retrying (`Retrying`): a cause that passes by nature - a live holder, a 429, a
  provider's pause - retried while it lasts, as long as its own answer says to wait; a failure retried while it is a new
  one, by its digest; and a final one ended at once.
- `Text\`: every regular expression made by one maker on .NET's linear-time engine, with no timeout, a construct that
  engine lacks refused by name (`LinearRegex`) - none source-generated, whose matcher backtracks - and each `\z` of a
  pattern with groups compiled as `(?:\Z\z)`, the same end, at which that engine keeps the groups it loses at a lone
  `\z` after a final line feed; a match sought from where a reader stands, the pattern's `\A` there, for the `\G` that
  engine lacks (`LinearRegex.MatchFrom`); and two sequences diffed by one owner with no edit bound - anchors that occur
  once on each side first, Myers' linear-space algorithm where a region has none (`SequenceDiff`).

Four owners gained members of the same kind. A one-line message names every item that fits its room and says where the
whole list is (`Output\Names.Line`). JSON is read, written and walked at any depth (`Json\JsonDepth`, and
`Json\JsonWalk` on an explicit stack, each place's path spelt only when it is asked for). A stream is hashed as it is
read (`FileContentHash.OfStreamAsync`), and a file's first line is read whole whatever its length
(`FileLines.FirstLineWholeAsync`). And the one YAML reader loads a document however deep it nests: its event scan
measures the nesting - the deepest it reached, where the text later stops reading as YAML - and YamlDotNet's model then
reads those events on a thread whose stack holds that depth (`DeepCalls.RunSized`), so an agent's frontmatter nested a
hundred thousand deep is read, or refused for what it holds, and never ends the process. An alias is the node its anchor
names, never a copy; a reader's own rule refuses one where its files write each part out (`YamlRules`: a workflow's
definition and a pubspec do); and a key that holds an alias of a mapping or a list, or of an anchor not yet written, is
refused, since the model would hash it without end.

### The platform layer

`HostPlatform`, `FilePermissionsFactory` and `ProcessTableFactory` are where the tool learns
which operating system it runs on and builds what differs by it. Everything above them depends
on `IHostPlatform`, `IFilePermissions`, `IProcessTable`, `IProcessRunner` and `IFileSystem`.
Below that seam a few primitives ask the runtime for one fact each, where nothing else is
asked - `PhysicalFileSystem`, `ProcessRunner`, `DetachedProcessLauncher`, `Containment` (the
session, group, signal and job-object calls containment is made of, and the choice between them
that `ContainExec` places a child through, and the one walk that ends a process with its tree,
each process it ends kept in what its caller gives it, for that caller to wait for as it needs), `UserState`,
`WslDiskImages`, `CMakeToolchainReader`, `ProcessContext` (the process's current directory),
`AgentChildEnvironment.Own` (the tool's own environment, which an agent's child would inherit),
`SystemWebNames` (a host name's addresses) and `HarnessFetch.Connecting` (the sockets the harness's
own fetch connects through), and the command that holds a host awake.

A file is read through one stream (`IFileSystem.OpenRead`) and written whole by one of two atomic writes, each writing
a temporary file beside the target and renaming it over the target: `IFileSystem.WriteAtomic`, handed a stream, for
what is made as it is written - a record, a text - and `WriteAllBytesAtomicAsync` for bytes already in hand, which a
tree sync, a fold's copy and a mutation write, waiting between its attempts without holding a thread. A file either
replaces keeps its mode (`IFilePermissions.CopyMode`: on Unix a script its execute bit, a secret its owner alone). A whole text or
a whole file's bytes is read and a text written by a convenience over those (`WholeFiles`), so a double that changes
how a file reads or writes changes it for every caller, whatever form the caller takes it in. A state file
(`JsonStateFile.Read`, `JsonStateFile.Write`) is parsed straight off that stream and serialized straight onto it,
never held as one text: a codebase graph's link result runs to tens of megabytes, and held as text it costs twice its
size again, in buffers the runtime's shared pool keeps. A file is renamed into place as POSIX renames, on Windows too
(`Win32Files.TryReplace`): one who holds the old file open - every read here shares its deletion - goes on reading it
while the new one takes its name, where Windows' own rename is refused while the old file is open at all, so a writer
could not replace a record another sync was streaming. A holder that shares nothing - a virus
scanner reading a file just written, an indexer holding one for minutes - is waited out instead,
through `Retrying`: the rename is tried again for as long as Windows reports a sharing or a lock
violation, or a look at either file finds another program holding it, each wait told naming the
file held (`PhysicalFileSystem`'s `told`), the waits doubling from 10 ms to five minutes, no count
of tries ending it; any other refusal is tried once more and raised where it meets the same state
again, and a directory standing at the destination, which no wait moves, is
refused at once. Every path's links are followed by one walk (`LinkPaths.Resolve`), realpath's,
each link once and no count of links: a chain however long is followed to its end, and only links
leading back to one still being followed end it, as a cycle. Where the system itself follows a
path, its own bound on a chain of links is its fact, met there. The room a path has is measured
where that walk leads it (`PhysicalFileSystem.MeasuredAt`), then at the nearest directory there
that exists. A volume that
cannot rename so - FAT, some shares - is renamed Windows' own way. Off Windows, a read refuses a pipe, a socket or a
device before it opens one (`UnixFiles`, the runtime's own stat, where .NET's attributes call each a plain file): a
pipe's open waits for a writer, past any stop.
A walk that must not stop at what it cannot read (`EnumerateReachableFiles`) goes a directory at a time, passing by
and naming one beneath it that cannot be read.

A platform-specific implementation is created only where behaviour genuinely
differs. Today that is three families of behaviour.

**File permissions**: making a file readable only by its owner, deciding whether a file
is a program at all, and whether other users can read or change a file. Unix answers
these with mode bits; Windows answers them with access lists and file extensions. Hence
a POSIX implementation and a Windows implementation, and no third.

**The process table**: what else is running on this machine, with each process's parent,
its start time and its command line, which is what a leg's contention check reads, and the
full path of the program it runs, which is how an update tells a session of the installation
it would replace from a program of the same name installed elsewhere - a command line need
not name its program by a path at all, and a process may write its own name and line over, as
node running Claude Code calls itself `claude` on Linux and macOS.
Windows publishes it through WMI, Linux through `/proc`, macOS through `ps` - whose name for a
process is the first word it was started with, never its program - and libproc's
`proc_pidpath`, which names the program. The kernel's own answers (`IProcessKernel`: `/proc`'s
files, libproc's path) sit behind a seam of their own, so a test scripts the ones a machine
cannot be made to give - another user's program, which Linux keeps from this user, a process
that ended, a zombie - and the table carries each as none. Behind the
seam so that nothing above it branches on the operating system to find out, and so a test
can say what the machine was running without the machine having to be running it.

**The input watch**: what a leg's work hears change among its inputs while it runs. On
Linux every watch of a process goes through one inotify instance the process calls itself
(`InotifyHub`); elsewhere, and on a Linux whose C library does not give those calls, through
.NET's watcher (`FileSystemWatcherKind`), each watched directory then taking an instance of
its own on Linux. `WatchKinds` chooses, in one place, from `IHostPlatform`.

### Process execution

`IProcessRunner` takes arguments as a **list**, never a command line string.
Shell quoting is therefore not part of the system. This is not a style
preference: a neighbouring repository measured a shell-string invocation whose
empty variable expanded into `rsync -a --delete / /`, ran for 70 minutes and
reported exit 0.

Child output is decoded, and child input encoded, as UTF-8 on every platform. Left to
its default, Windows decodes redirected output with the console's legacy code page, so
a path such as `C:\Users\João` printed by git would reach the harness garbled on
Windows alone.

A missing working directory is reported as exactly that. Linux and macOS report it
with the same error number as a missing executable, which would otherwise surface as
"git is not installed". It is looked for before the start, and again where a start
fails: one a deletion took away between the two is said as gone, in the same words,
never as an interpreter or loader the program needs being missing.

A caller's handler for the lines a child writes is handed no more once it fails, and the
stream is still read to its end, what the handler raised being raised once the child has
gone. Left to stop reading, a child writing more than a pipe holds blocks on it, and a
host's agent - whose input is held open, so that it can tell the machine that asked has
gone - never ends: a file read back from a host whose content was refused part way left
its command waiting until something stopped it.

A program named without a path is looked up in the `PATH` directories and nowhere else -
the `PATH` the child is given, which ends with the directories the survey found a leg's
programs in, and begins with any a tool's `minVersion` raised. Left to the runtime, it would
be looked for beside the running executable and in the current directory first, and the
current directory is usually the repository, so a file committed there under a tool's name
would run in place of the tool. On Windows a name
without an extension starts only `<name>.exe`, never a batch file, whose arguments cmd.exe
would parse a second time, and a path without one starts that path with `.exe` added. A
program a leg's configuration names by a relative path is read from the directory its phase
starts in - a step's working directory, the test runner's - never from wherever the harness was
started: for a leg on a worktree those are different copies of the same file.

A request can ask for a child **contained**: what it started ends with it, at its own end as at a
stop, and a signal to the harness does not reach it. A process has to be where it is contained
before it runs a line of its own, and `Process.Start` offers no moment between a child's making
and its start on any system, so the runner - the one owner of processes - starts a contained child
through a copy of this tool that puts itself there first: the hidden `contain-exec` command, which
on Linux and macOS makes itself the leader of a new session and process group (`setsid`) and then
becomes the program by its whole path (`execv`, under the same process id - never `execvp`, which
runs a file with no interpreter line under `/bin/sh` where any other start refuses it), and on
Windows joins the named job
object the runner made and starts the program in a process group of its own, handing the streams
it was given on to it. The step says nothing on the runner's channel until the runner writes it
one byte saying its connection was taken (`ContainExec.Taken`), so a step seen to end with its
connection not taken said nothing, however late the system would have handed over a connection
made just before its end, and is given up at once. On Windows the job is ended as the child ends or is stopped, and every
member goes with it - one whose own security refuses another its end among them, since the job's end asks nothing of
it, and each is waited for by a handle that only waits and asks when it was created; and since its members also end when its last handle closes, what a killed
engine leaves behind ends with it there. On Linux and macOS the runner ends the child's session as
the child ends or is stopped - every process still in it, and at a stop every one still in the
child's tree, as the process table names each parent (`SampledProcess.ParentId`, no start compared), read before anything is signalled, asked to end with SIGTERM and waited for while
any of it stands, a zombie - which nothing may ever reap - standing for none and a process still in
its exit standing until it is one, one the harness may not signal - another user's - not waited for,
and the group for none once every member it is listed to hold is one, never by a signal alone, which
macOS passes a process in its exit over for - told every five minutes, and killed at what is left of the child's time limit,
or at once where a sweep ends what a killed run left, that run's bound having passed with it.
What still stands is held still before it is killed: the group as one, each member of the first
reading still that very process - known by its id and its start read as that reading was taken - and
then, round by round until a round takes none, every process the system names in the session, or the
group, and every child of a process held, so what a member outside the group started after the first
reading goes too; one whose session or group cannot be asked - in its creation or its exit, anywhere on
the machine - is never waited on, one of the run's in its creation reached as its held parent's child
or once all is killed. The system is
read in place - its own listing of every process with its parent - never through a program: on macOS,
for as long as a child of a process stands stopped, that process's runtime spins over reaping its
children and holds the lock every start of a program takes, so a reading through `ps` there, with the
group - which may hold the process's own child - held, never began, and every start of the process
waited behind it. The process running the end is never held, nor walked below. Once all it
killed has gone the system is read again the same way, and what stands in the session, or the group,
is held and killed in turn until a look finds none: a child whose creation was under way as its parent
was held joins the listing only after the last round, and its parent's kill ends that call or leaves
it standing there. Such a child of a member outside the group, born outside it, is reached by nothing
once its parent has gone.
Nothing a session's end does acts on the process running it: a session, or a group, that holds that
process, or whose leader it descends from, is refused before anything is signalled - the asking is
taken for a cancel and gone on through, and the hold after it would stop that process where it
stands with everything it runs in - and left for a process outside it to end.
Whatever a stop or a container's end ends is waited for until it has gone before the output's end
is looked for (`EndedProcesses`): the system answers a kill before the process's end has run - a
descendant still unmapping its memory or running down its handles holds the write end of the
child's output for that while - and a process the stop itself ended, taken then for one the child
left running, was said to hold the output on a run whose stop had ended everything. So each process
ended is kept as it is ended - on Windows by a handle, the job's members listed and kept before the
job is ended, each checked to be in it by its own handle; on Linux and macOS by its id and its start,
read while it is held still (SIGSTOP) before anything is killed - and waited for, told every five
minutes and with no grace of any length: on Windows until its handle is signalled, which comes only
once its handle table has run down, and on Linux and macOS until no process carries its id with its
start or that process is a zombie, whose descriptors are closed, whether or not anything ever reaps
it - its start read through its exit too, while it is still closing what it held: macOS lets nothing
take a reference to a process from the moment it enters its exit, before its descriptors are closed,
so there the start is read from the kernel's own record of it, kept until it is reaped, and never
from the runtime, whose reading refuses such a process. On Windows the job, and a stopped tree, are listed again once every process kept has gone, for a
child one made while it was being ended - a process of the tree a look again passes over said once, with the first
walk's, in what the stop could not end (`EndedProcesses.Refused`, read once the wait is over). Then
the output is read until every character the child wrote has been, to its end or until a look finds
the pipe holding nothing while something still holds it open (`ProcessRunner.StreamCapture`: each
look, once the child has ended, ends the read that waits - a read ended so has taken nothing, the
runtime ending a read only before it takes a byte - and asks the pipe through `PipeBytes`, no read
waiting on it, by a peek on Windows and by poll on Linux and macOS; never by the read's task, which on
Windows waits for a pool thread to make the read while what the child wrote sits in the pipe, and a
pipe holding bytes, or one every writer has let go of, is read on); what a leftover writes after
that is its
own, said in `ProcessResult.OutputHeld` and not read: a process
that made a session of its own away from the child's tree is not reached, and nothing waits for
what it holds. On macOS, where the isolation keeps no process namespace, such a process of an
isolated command's outlives its launch and goes on writing the places it was given; every file
operation of the tool's over those places - a fold, a hand-over, evidence kept, a removal, a sync -
acts relative to directories it holds (`UnfollowedFiles`, `HeldDirectory`), so a link it swaps in
meanwhile reaches nothing of the tool's. git's own removal of a worktree, which a forced
`delete-worktree` still runs (`git worktree remove --force --force`), walks the tree by path, and is
where such a process still meets the tool's work. A process table that cannot be read - macOS's is read through `ps`, which a session
that has used up every process it may start leaves unable to start - takes nothing from the stop:
the group is still asked and then killed by its id, which needs no table, the tree is still ended,
and what went unreached is said in the result (`ProcessResult.Uncontained`), or, where the caller
gave up, carried by the cancellation it is thrown (`ProcessStoppedException.Uncontained`) and said
in its message. A process killed there - a crash, `kill -9` - ends nothing
of the sessions it started, so each one a step of an orchestrator starts is recorded while it runs,
by the runner through the tool's own records: once the child is placed in its session and before
it is said to have started, `<step>/children/<session>.json` in the step's own directory - its
session (the child's process id), the child's start stamp - said by `contain-exec` of its own start
on the channel, just before it becomes the program, which keeps it, so a child that ends at once
is recorded all the same - its program, and the process that
started it with that process's machine and stamp (`ChildSessions`, the request's
`SessionRecord`) - and taken back once the runner has ended the session. The same record, with
`group: true`, names the process group a run's machine step's legs' work leads (below: a bound child
under a `ProcessScope`), taken back once the child has ended and nothing is left in its group. A
record that cannot be
written - one whose child's start nothing can read among them - is a start that failed: the child
is ended as a stop ends it, and never said to have started, the failure saying what that end could
not end beside why the record was not written; a defect that keeps one from being written, a record that
would not read back among them, ends the child too, and is raised as it is. Every command
over an orchestrator - `create-`, `list-` and `delete-orchestrator`, each agent verb, and each run
verb over a run already made - first
sweeps its records, before it reads anything else of it: a session or group whose starter still stands is
its starter's and is left; one whose starter has gone is ended as the runner ends a contained
child's session at its end - a group by its own members and the tree its leader stands over, never
the session it shares with its starter (`Containment.EndSessionAsync`, `group`) -
its record removed and the end said in the command's lines and in its document's `ended` where it
answers with one, where anything was left in it - but only where the process carrying its id still
has the recorded start, or no process carries the id at all: none is given an id a session or a
group still carries, so what a leader killed with the engine's tree handed on is still found by
it. An id given to a later process ends nothing, and that record simply goes. A session or group
that holds the command sweeping - it runs in it, or descends from its leader, read up the chain of
parents the walk's own refusal reads (`Containment.TheCallersChain`) - is never ended from inside:
nothing in it is signalled, the refusal is said, and its record kept for a command run from outside
it to end - kept for real: the sweep answers what it kept so beside what it ended (`ChildSweep`), and
a command that would lose that record or take the run inside it refuses (13), naming the record and
changing nothing - `delete-orchestrator`, whose deletion would take the record with the run's
directory, and every command that makes this process a run's engine, whose engine would run inside
what the next command from outside ends: a new run's start (`run-orchestrator`,
`FlowSessions.CreateAsync`) and a session of a run already made (`resume-orchestrator`,
`answer-orchestrator`, each claiming the run's owner, `FlowSessions.ClaimAsync`). Each refuses over
a sweep taken at the act itself, so the record it refuses over is never older than the act: the
start and the claim sweep every run of the repository, as `list-orchestrator` does, inside the
section that decides the run's owner, once the last look at it has found it gone or none and
before the run is made or the owner taken (`ProcessOwner.Claim`, `taking`) - an owner seen gone
there cannot come back, and a live one is never claimed - so a refusal leaves the owner file as it
was; and `delete-orchestrator` sweeps its orchestrator again inside its section right before the
removal. An owner seen standing as the command began and gone since, one an answer was handed to
and waited on among them, is swept with the rest, what it left ended before the new session runs,
and a record kept refuses the act; every other command goes on with the warning. A command that
sweeps more than once - as it begins, and again at the act - says each thing its sweeps say of a
record once, and keeps each end once in its document's `ended`: one guard in `ChildSessions`
(`SaidFirst`) over every line a sweep says - the record kept, one that does not read, one this
system never writes, one that could not be removed, and the end - and over the end it keeps, so a
later sweep that finds a record as before says and keeps nothing more of it.
`stop-orchestrator --now` sweeps again once it has ended the engine and its tree, and says what it
ended: what outlived that end. A tree is ended by holding each process of it still before any is
killed (`Containment.EndTree`, below), and the system hangs up a group that loses its last parent in
the session while one of its members is held, so a leftover may die of that hangup with the engine,
and is then not said. A
record that does not read as one is said and left, and a starter on another machine is never taken
to have gone. Windows records nothing: its job already ends a killed starter's children.

A request can also carry an **isolation** (`ProcessRequest.Isolation`, a `ProcessIsolation`: a
mechanism and a profile), and an isolated child always starts through `contain-exec`, contained or
not - one that is not is placed as any other, in a group of its own on Linux and macOS - for
`contain-exec` is what places it: the runner hands `contain-exec`, after its separator, the mechanism's own command
line (`IIsolationMechanism.Command`) in the program's place - the program resolved by its whole
path first, its words after the mechanism's - so `contain-exec` becomes the mechanism, and the
mechanism the program, and no child runs outside it for an instant. Every mechanism is told the
same profile (`IsolationProfile`): the places hidden; the write rules in their order, parent first -
each writable root written, each place inside it written by nobody; the places read again inside a
hidden one (`Reopened`); a temporary directory of the child's own (`Temp`); the variables set inside
(`Environment`: `TMPDIR` and each declared tool cache's); the Unix sockets outside it reaches
(`Sockets`); and, of the places it names, the anchors (`IsolationProfile.Anchors`: every directory
above a guarded place and each writable root itself, `AnchorsOf`, each whose own holder is written).
The machine is read-only under each. What a mechanism holds of its own it says on its type
(`IIsolationMechanism`): whether a rule holds a place under every spelling a file system that
ignores letter case reaches it by (`HoldsEveryCase`), whether abstract sockets and signals are
scoped (`Scoped`) and what is left reached where not (`Leaves`), what its anchors cost
(`AnchorCost`), whether it gives the child a temporary directory of its own (`OwnTemp`), and whether
it takes a command handed to it from a process apart from it (`TakesHandedCommands`), and why a process inside it
cannot be held inside it as an outer layer of its own (`Unnested`). On Linux the
mechanism is the system's bubblewrap (`Bubblewrap`): the machine bound read-only (`--ro-bind / /`,
`--dev /dev`), a user namespace of its own allowing no further one (`--unshare-user
--disable-userns`) - a program's outer layer among them, for nothing is started inside it - a process namespace with its own `/proc` (`--unshare-pid --proc /proc`, so
`/proc/<id>/root` and `/proc/<id>/environ` reach no process outside), never `--die-with-parent`,
whose parent would be the thread that started the step; the launch's temporary directory bound at
`/tmp` and any read root under `/tmp` bound again read-only; then the profile's writes in its order,
the last mount at a place winning (`--bind-try` where written, `--ro-bind-try` where written by
nobody), each anchor among them by its depth bound onto itself as the nearest rule above it leaves
it, so it is a mount point inside, which the kernel keeps from being renamed or removed; then each
hidden place (an empty `tmpfs` over a directory, made read-only after any socket it holds is bound
into it; `/dev/null` read-only over a file), then the machine's own escapes the same way
(`IsolationPlatform.EscapeDirectories`: WSL's `/run/WSL` and `/mnt/wsl`, screen's `/run/screen`; the
user's runtime directory whole, `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` or `/run/user/<uid>`; each container engine's
socket, `IsolationPlatform.ContainerSockets`), every other socket of the profile's bound last at its
own path, and `WSL_INTEROP` unset. Where the kernel has Landlock's scope of abstract sockets and
signals (`Landlock`, its sixth version, Linux 6.12), `contain-exec --scope` enters it before it
becomes bubblewrap, so no process inside reaches an abstract socket outside or signals a process
outside; where it has not, the record's `leaves` says so (`Bubblewrap.Unscoped`). No
`--new-session`: `contain-exec`'s `setsid` made the child's session already, and a second would
take it out of the session a stop ends; the process tree the stop reads from outside sees every
process inside by its outside id. On macOS the mechanism is the system's own sandbox
(`SandboxExec`): `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec -p <profile> -D<NAME>=<path>... -- /usr/bin/env
<variables>... <program>`, its profile written for the child (`SandboxExec.Policy`) -
`(deny default)`, never `(allow default)`, which would leave LaunchServices free to start a program
outside every sandbox; then what a build, a test and a shell do as the user (its own processes
forked, run and signalled, the system's settings read by the names a build asks, never another
process's arguments or environment, a terminal, the network by address, the name resolver's socket,
the services that resolve names and trust certificates, every file read, and written only the
devices a shell writes); then the profile's own rules last, for the last rule an operation meets
holds - the temporary directory written, its Unix sockets bound and reached, each write rule in its
order (`allow file-write*` at a writable root, `deny file-write*` inside it), each hidden place
(`deny file-read* file-write*`), each reopened place read, each anchor (`deny file-write-unlink` of a
directory), each socket of the profile's reached (`network-outbound` to its `unix-socket`), and the
two file controls that write through a descriptor opened only to read (`F_MAKECOMPRESSED`,
`F_TRANSFEREXTENTS`). The sandbox meets a path as the file system names it, so each place is ruled
at its real spelling (`/var` is `/private/var`) and, where it is itself a link, at its own entry
too, and the anchors are those of the spellings; each spelling is handed over as a parameter, never
written into the profile's text. On Windows the mechanism is Microsoft's MXC process container
(`MxcProcessContainer`), made through MXC's own library (`Microsoft.Mxc.Sdk`, MIT, named in
`THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES` with every other package the tool carries): its command line is this tool
again - `isolate-exec --hidden <p>... --sealed|--writable <p>... --variable <NAME=value>... --
<program> <words>`, a step nobody types (`IsolateExec`) - so `contain-exec` starts it in the step's
job, and it starts the program inside a container of its own, handing on its input and handing back
its output, its error and its exit code; a container that cannot be made ends it with
`contain-exec`'s own failure code. The container grants nothing it is not told to
(`MxcProcessContainer.Files`): every fixed drive read, each writable root written, each place
written by nobody read, each hidden place denied outright (MXC's denied paths, which the machine's
container must support). It meets a place by its path alone, and refuses no rename alone, so each
anchor whose own holder the profile writes is read alone, and each entry it holds that no rule of
its own names written again as the profile has it: nothing is made or removed directly inside such
an anchor, so git makes no lock file in a `.git` that holds a sealed place, nor in a linked
worktree's directory under it - git add, commit, fetch and push fail there, in a worktree, over a
side-task's main tree and in a run's commit and push steps, which the record's `anchorCost` says
(`MxcProcessContainer.AnchorReadAlone`). The child has the environment the step was given and the
profile's variables, never the machine's, in which MXC sets a temporary directory of its own,
removed with the container (`OwnTemp`); the container's own user interface, with no clipboard and no
input sent to another window - with the interface turned off, every program that loads Windows'
user interface library ends `0xC0000142` before its first line; and the user's network, in and out,
the host's loopback among it. MXC is handed no socket: Windows' SSH agent is a named pipe. Which
mechanism the machine has is the platform's (`IIsolationPlatform`, `IsolationPlatform`): on Linux
the first `bwrap` in an absolute directory of the PATH outside the tree, 0.8 or newer, and none
where the user may write it or a directory above it, for the tool runs it outside before anything
is isolated; on macOS `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec` alone, never one the PATH names, where this process
runs inside no sandbox already (`sandbox_check`), for macOS starts none inside another - its
questions of the machine one seam a test answers anywhere (`MacSandboxHost`: the file there, the
sandbox already, the version of macOS a record names, each path's real spelling from `realpath`);
on Windows the container, where MXC's library says the machine has it and can deny a place
outright - its question one seam a test answers anywhere too (`WindowsContainerHost`: the library's
backends, and its version, which a record names). Both seams are the root's, registered beside the
other registrations that observe the operating system, so a test answers them through the tool's
own registrations too. Each is proved once per process, on the tree's
own file system under its runs directory (`isolation-probe-<id>`, removed after), by a probe started
exactly as every isolated child is - each of its programs - bubblewrap's version, each canary and
start it tries - run to its end with no bound of the tool's own (`Waits`), told every five minutes
while it runs and ended only by a stop - a canary in a hidden place unread, by its name and by another
case of its directory's; a place written by nobody unwritten, by either spelling; a place outside
every open one unwritten; an open place written - each checked from outside, through `sh` on Linux
and macOS and through `cmd.exe` on Windows, a run for each, and why not with the remedy where it
fails (Ubuntu's `apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns` named with the `bwrap-userns-restrict`
profile; on Windows the builds MXC needs, or WSL 2). On Windows each of node, git and Git Bash's
`sh` - on the PATH outside the tree, `sh` else beside the git found - is then started inside the
container and must end 0 having said something; one that does not is no mechanism, named with its
path and how it ended, a status the system ended it with written in hexadecimal, and one not on the
machine is not asked. MXC 1.0.1 ends every program of Git Bash's with `0xC0000142`, so a Windows
with Git for Windows has none yet. What a launch's profile holds is the agents' isolation's, below.

A request can ask instead for a child **bound** to the harness's life (`ProcessRequest.Bound`):
on Windows it is placed through `contain-exec` too, in the one job object the process holds for its
whole life - whichever operation's runner starts it, though each operation is given services of its
own - which ends every member when its last handle closes; so the harness ending in any way, a hard
kill among them, ends
the child and all it started at once. Its own end and a stop are as any other child's: nothing is
terminated as it ends, and what it leaves running lives on until the harness ends - so, on every
system, its output is read, once it has ended - and at a stop once everything the stop ended has
gone - until every character it wrote has been - to its
end, or until a look finds the pipe holding nothing with no read waiting on it - as a contained child's is
once its container has: what still holds the output then is one of those leftovers, a server its
phase started in the background, or at a stop a process the stop could not end, said in
`ProcessResult.Uncontained` - and the output's holder is then said, as its wait is told, to be such a
process or one the child left running - whose later output is its own and is said not read
(`ProcessResult.OutputHeld`), so the run is held neither for as long as it lives nor cut short of
anything the child wrote; the child's own last
line is handed on. Every phase of
a leg a dispatcher runs on its own machine - a build, a test, a runner's step, a mutation arm's
run, a set-up's down line - is bound, and so is its `keepAwake` command: a dispatcher killed where
it stood once left its legs' test runners running for minutes, each holding a heavy leg's room. A
set-up's `up` line is not: what it brings up is shared, held across runs, and ended by its `down`
line. A child held in a job - contained or bound - is given build servers of its own, where its
environment names none: the compiler's program-database server listens at an endpoint named for
the job (`_MSPDBSRV_ENDPOINT_`), and the build engine leaves no node for a later build
(`MSBUILDDISABLENODEREUSE=1`) - a server a member starts ends with the job, and one shared with
another dispatcher's builds would be taken from them mid-build. An endpoint named for a job of the
harness's own is replaced too: a harness a bound phase of another started inherits that one's, and
a server its own children started there would end with its job while the outer builds still used
it; an endpoint the user named is kept. The ssh or wsl.exe that carries a leg to a host is bound
too (`HostCommand.Bound`): the host's leg ends when its input does. On Linux
and macOS a bound child starts as any other: an interrupt or a termination signal given to the
harness ends it with the harness's stop, a hang-up of its terminal reaches it as it reaches the
harness, and a kill of the harness alone does not reach it - `stop-run --now` ends the harness with
its whole tree. Save under a **process scope** (`ProcessScope`), which a run's machine step and a
reason step's measure call open around their legs (`FlowStepLegs`), flowing with the operation and seen by nothing outside it: there
every child but a contained one is started apart from the terminal, so the engine's first Ctrl+C -
a safe pause - leaves the builds running, and a bound child's group is recorded in the step's
directory as a contained child's session is, while anything is in it, so a killed engine leaves
none of it unrecorded; a stop ends the group at once with the tree. On Windows a child keeps the
console of its own it always has, the job binds a bound one, and nothing is recorded.

Whether the program started is said on a channel of the runner's own (`--status`), never in the
program's streams or an exit code a program could give too: a program that cannot start is
reported as one that never ran (`ExecutableNotFoundException`, `ProgramStartException`, worded as
for any other start, a program being written tried again as any start is), and the child is said
to have started (`OnStarted`) only once the step has placed it. The group alone, apart from the
terminal but within the session, is the lesser level a request asks for by name
(`ApartFromTerminal`), and only Linux and macOS start a child through the step for it: an
interruption typed at the harness's terminal is sent to a group, and that group is not the child's.
On Windows such a child starts as any other, since a child started with no window already has a
console of its own that an interruption typed at the harness's never reaches. A child apart from
the terminal is stopped by its process tree, as any other, and on Linux and macOS by its group as
well, at once, which reaches what its tree handed on; what it leaves at its own end is left. A
tree, and the group beside it, is ended by one walk (`Containment.EndTree`) - for a stop, for
`stop-run --now` and `stop-orchestrator --now`, and for a host agent's last resort alike. It never
acts on the process running it: a tree whose root is that process, or one it descends from - read
up its own chain of parents, each the parent the walk itself reads - on Linux and macOS the one the
system names now, a child being handed on as its parent ends, before that parent's id is given out;
on Windows one made no later than its child, as the walk orders a creator and its child (below) -
is refused before anything is held or ended, which `--now` answers as could not be ended,
its owner kept, and the last resort as left. On Linux
and macOS it holds each process still (SIGSTOP) before it takes that process's children - once it
has stopped, a process starts no other, and a child of it is never reaped and its id given out
before the walk acts on it; the table of every process with its parent - Linux's `/proc`, macOS's
listing of every process - is read once a round however deep the tree, each child asked again once
its parent is held, until a round takes none, and a child the table names that no hold answers yet
is asked again, paced and told every five minutes, until it is held or the table no longer names it.
A process stops only once a call it is inside has returned, so a child whose creation was already
under way when its parent was held may join the table after the round that took none: nothing an
unprivileged process may ask closes that instant, and a contained child's session, or a group, is
the end that reaches what its tree started in it - a session's end reads the system again once all it
killed has gone. Then the group, as one before it is listed and each member by its own
id, and only then it kills it all: the group as one first, while it stands, so a member its listing did not show - one
`/proc` hides, or whose reading failed - goes with it and is never left held still, each member killed by the group
alone, since its id may be given out again once the group is killed, and every other process by its own id, the child
last (`Containment.HeldStill`, the one order a session's end kills in too). On Windows, where nothing is held still, it
ends each process as it finds it, the root first - each process its caller holds the handle it was
created with for kept by a copy of that handle, which ends and waits for it whatever its own security
refuses another: the child the process runner ends, at a stop or where its start could not be read,
by the handle the runtime got as it was created, and the program the tool's own step created for a
bound, contained or isolated child by the handle `contain-exec` got as it created it, whose value
`contain-exec` says on its channel before it says the program placed and the runner copies out of it
while it stands (`Containment.CopiedFrom`); the process `--now` or a last resort ends is opened by its
id, all they know of it - a child being one the list Windows keeps of every process names as created
by a process of the tree and made after it, and the very one the list named, as its own handle's
creation time says, so an id taken since the list was read is never ended. Made after is read by the
sequence number Windows gives each process as it creates it (`ProcessSequenceNumber`, counted up once
a boot and never moved by the clock) where both could be opened to read theirs, and by their creation
times, the clock's, where either could not (`CreationOrder`, the one order of a creator and its child,
which the chain of parents above reads too). A process of the tree that cannot be opened - one running
as another user, one whose own security refuses the harness its end, or one gone as it was reached -
is passed over, its refusal said once, and still has its children taken from the reading that found
it, by its listed id and creation time alone, no right asked of it, as a root that could not be ended
has its own from the first reading. What a stop could not end it says beside what a container could
not reach (`ProcessResult.Uncontained`, and `ProcessStoppedException.Uncontained`, which the stop its caller gave up is
thrown carries in place of a result), and what then holds the child's
output is said to be such a process or one the child left running, never a refusal taken for a
leftover (`ProcessResult.OutputHeld`). That is data of the run, worded once by the runner, and said by
the caller that owns the operation's output - once, with its own context, from the result and from the
stop alike (`UnreachedSaying`, read where the run is awaited, inside any wait over it that would end
at the caller's token with a cancellation of its own) - and by no second teller of the process's, so
nothing is said twice: a leg's phase on the leg's line (`PhaseRunner`); a leg run on its host on
the leg's line, under the command running it (`RemoteLegRunner`); a sync's request, a hold and
`host-exec`'s command under their command, naming the host (`RemoteSyncTransport`,
`HoldAwakeRegistry`, `HostExecService`, with WSL naming its default distribution); a machine's `keepAwake` on the leg's line (`KeepAwake`); git and gh under
their own names, by the command line asked (`GitClient`, `GhProcess`); the tool's probes under the
tool or the command they serve, naming what ran - ssh's settings and shell probe, a program a
connection, a lookup, an inspection or a provisioning runs on a host, a copy asked its version, an
emulator's witness, `vswhere`, `vcvarsall.bat`, the process table's reader, a stopped isolation
probe, ctest describing the tests, `dotnet tool list`, the drop of WSL's page cache - and a
set-up's line under its direction (`SetUpService`). A caller with no output of its own for the
operation is handed its caller's way of saying it and names what it ran: git's question of the
variables it reads (`GitLocalVariables`), handed git's or gh's; the build's questions of a compiler
and of ninja (`CompilerVersionProbe`, `NinjaDeadOutputCheck`, `NinjaDependencyCheck`,
`NinjaRebuildGraph`), handed the build's line or, through the arms' builder each sweep makes over its
own output (`MutationService.Builder`), a mutation worker's; npm's client and Claude
Code's installation (`NpmClient`, `ClaudeCodeInstall`), handed the command that asks Claude Code
ready. A host's commands (`HostCommandRunner`) hand it on as it came, a pinned ssh call run again
without its pin with what both attempts could not reach or end; an isolation probe's trial reports
it as why no mechanism proved itself, since a container that leaves a process of the trial running
proves nothing; Claude Code's launch says it as its end's notice and keeps it in the step's result. The
root hands the operation's output to the process table and the isolation platform it builds
(`ServiceRegistration`), which have no other. The
walk keeps each process it ends in what its caller gives it (`EndedProcesses`), and each
caller waits for what it needs: a stop waits until every process it ended has gone before the
child's output's end is looked for (above), as a contained child's end does, so what is said to hold
the output then is only ever what the stop did not end; `--now` waits for the recorded process
alone, the rest of its tree let go of as it is ended; and a host agent's last resort, and a child
whose start could not be read, wait for none. No leg is contained: a `build`, `test` or `run` typed by hand starts its legs' phases bound on
Windows, as above, and as any other child elsewhere.

### Paths come from git

Every repository path the harness holds — the tree a command acts on, the main
checkout, each worktree — comes from git, in the single form git resolves it to, with
symbolic links followed. A directory the user typed is only ever used to tell git where
to start. If one root were spelled as typed and another as git resolved it, the same
checkout would compare unequal to itself wherever a link is involved: macOS keeps its
temporary directory under the `/var` link, and any repository cloned beneath a linked
directory behaves the same way.

`--directory` is resolved to an absolute path, and confirmed to exist, once, before any
command runs.

An engine's session asks git where each of its trees is once (`EngineSession`, `SessionTrees`):
the run's main checkout and each agent's tree cannot move while the engine holds the run, so a
tree located from its own root - its top, the repository's worktrees, the main checkout's git
directory, an agent's repository's mark, what every load of a context asks
(`RepositoryLocator`) - is kept for the rest of the session and handed to every layer its work
passes through, its step runners and the agent and worktree services they ask, rather than asked
again at each. So are the directory the main checkout's repository keeps its objects in, however
it was asked, and an agent's repository's mark where its main checkout lends it its objects -
found by the locator or by the telling of an agent's repository (`AgentRepositories.IsAtAsync`),
and taken by the other, so a tree a deletion tells and then loads is asked of once - and the
files of each commit a tree is made at, by the commit's id (`WorktreeRoom.ForFilesAsync`). Its
configuration is still read where it always is, for it is the tree's file. A
tree the session makes, deletes or makes again is dropped by the one owner of the making and the
deleting of trees (`WorktreeService`), and found anew by the next asking; what was kept of a tree
is served only while its root still holds its own `.git`, looked at as it is served, so a `.git`
taken away by anything else - a person, another command - leaves the directory asked of anew, as
whatever repository encloses it answers for it, and the fact is dropped; a directory inside a
tree is never kept, for it may become a tree of its own; and the session's scope flows with the
work it starts alone, so no other command or session is answered from it, and it ends with the
session.

git's messages are matched in two places only: telling "not a repository" apart from
"git could not look", and "not a gitdir" apart from the same when a directory among a
worktree's submodule repositories is examined - both questions - and a workflow source's fetch
or listing telling "not there" from "not reached". Every git the tool starts runs with
`LC_ALL=C` but one that runs a repository's hooks on purpose (a commit step's commit, a push) and
one git runs them for, set at the one place for every git start (`GitOwnSettings.Untranslated`) -
the client's (`GitOwnSettings.Apply`), the question that names the variables every git is started
without (`GitLocalVariables`), and the isolation probe's `git --version` alike - never by a caller:
a question is answered in the words being matched. Those commands keep the person's locale, the
ones git runs hooks for whether a hook runs or not, so a hook
behaves as in their shell - a JVM tool's file names, Ruby's default encoding, a shell's
character classes and lengths, a server's hooks over ssh that `SendEnv LC_*` would forward to -
and their messages reach the person in their language: each command `githooks(5)` names as
running one (`GitHooks.Runners` - `am`, `commit`, `merge`, `pull`, `rebase`, `cherry-pick`,
`revert`, `checkout`, `switch`, `clone`, `worktree add`, `push`, `receive-pack`, `send-email`,
`gc`, `p4 submit`), by its subcommand after git's own options (`GitHooks.MayRun`), read by the one
grammar of them the agents' policy reads too (`GitGlobalOptions.SubcommandAt`): each option that
takes the next word as its value - `-C`, `-c`, `--config-env`, `--git-dir`, `--work-tree`,
`--namespace` and the other long ones that name a place or a list - is passed over with it, so
`git --git-dir /r/.git commit` is a commit, never a command named `/r/.git`. The two hooks
it names no command for - reference-transaction, which any command that moves a ref runs, and
post-index-change, which any that writes the index runs - make no command one of them: every
command that writes would be, and no git of the tool's runs a hook but where it runs them on
purpose.

### Reading config.json

The file is edited by hand, so it is checked as it is read, and every problem is reported
at once, with the line it concerns where the parser knows it:

- An unknown key is an error. A misspelled setting that is silently dropped reverts to
  its default while the file plainly appears to set it.
- A key written twice is an error, in any case: read, the file kept the last copy's value and
  dropped the first's without a word.
- A member the reader never reads, one marked `[JsonIgnore]`, is no key of the file's: a key naming
  it is refused like any other. Left to the serializer, its value is skipped without a word.
- `null` is refused wherever the model does not allow it, including inside lists and
  maps, which the serializer does not check on its own. Loaded, it would fail much later
  as a crash in whatever first read it.
- A list whose absence means every one of what it names, or a set the tool chooses, is refused
  given empty, by one rule and in one wording: a runner's `legs` and `steps`; a tool's `platforms`,
  `toolchains`, `legs`, `processors` and `emulators`; a toolchain's `platforms`; an emulator's
  `phases`; `ci.workflows`; `test.inputs`; a project's `targets` and `rebuildableFormats`; a
  platform's `toolSearchDirectories`; `agentWebSearch.defaults`. Read as the key left out, a
  runner's `"legs": []` synced the tree to every host and ran on every leg, for a list naming
  none, as `--legs` given no name would have. Left out, each still means what it did, and a list a
  caller builds empty in code reads as left out. A list whose empty form means none - such as `sync.neverTransfer`, `sync.exclude` or
  `contention.buildTools` - takes `[]` as that.
- A key nothing reads is refused, saying so: a test section's `configs`, which `init` once wrote
  and nothing ever read - each leg builds and tests the one config its `config` names - and `exec`,
  whose named commands no command ever ran: each is a set-up's line under `setUp` now, saying so.
  Refused even empty, since the file plainly appears to declare commands.
- References are resolved: a leg naming an undeclared host or emulator, an emulator that
  runs programs for another processor than the leg's, a success pattern that does not
  compile, a commit template placeholder no variable declares.
- **Any depth, linear patterns.** The file is read with no depth bound of the reader's own
  (`JsonConfigOptions`, `JsonDepth`): a value whose shape holds any depth - a client's
  `requestExtras` - is read however deep, and one a typed place cannot hold is refused for that
  shape, never for its depth. Its patterns are compiled by `LinearRegex`, matched in time linear
  in the text with no timeout, and a construct that matcher lacks - a backreference, a lookahead
  or lookbehind - is refused where the file is read, naming the pattern and the construct.
- **A toolchain CMake builds with names its compiler**: `CC` or `CXX` under `env`,
  `CMAKE_C_COMPILER`, `CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER` or `CMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE` under `cacheVars`, or a
  `compilerId` CMake must configure it with. One naming none is refused, because CMake then takes
  whatever compiler it finds first - how a leg named `msvc` built with MinGW's gcc on every run until
  `CC` was declared - and the build directory guard has nothing to hold a later build to. A
  toolchain only .NET or Dart projects build with names none: those resolve their own compilers,
  and its `cacheVars` are that build's properties. `init`'s `msvc` toolchain names `cl`.
- **Every CMake configure is asked which compilers it resolved**, through the file API: the build
  writes the `toolchains-v1` query into its build directory before configuring, notes the answers
  already there, and reads the one that configure wrote. Each leg's line names what CMake answered -
  `compiler: MSVC 19.51.36231 (C, CXX)`, one entry per compiler with the languages it serves -
  whatever the verdict, and `--json` carries it as `compilers`. A configure that fails answers
  nothing about the compilers - CMake 4 writes an error index in its place, and leaves the last
  successful configure's answer where it was - so it names none, never the ones an earlier
  configure resolved; told apart by what was there before, never by the times in the names, which
  a clock that stepped back would reorder. It travels beside the detail rather than inside it, so a
  leg a host ran is named once on the machine that reports it. A toolchain's `compilerId` -
  `{"C": "MSVC", "CXX": "MSVC"}`, in CMake's own ids - holds the build to it: a compiler CMake
  configured that contradicts it fails the leg before anything is built, and a declared language
  CMake identified no compiler for leaves it `unwitnessed`, naming why - an older CMake writes no
  answer, and a misspelled language is never answered. The answer holds what the top-level
  directory holds, so a language only a subdirectory enables - C, where a C++ project fetches
  googletest, whose own `project()` declares C and C++ - comes with no id: with its compiler's
  path where CMake caches one, and under a Visual Studio generator, which caches none, with no
  path either. A leg declaring the C it built with was left `unwitnessed` while its configure log
  named that compiler. CMake keeps each language's identification once for the whole build
  directory, in `CMakeFiles/<version>/CMake<language>Compiler.cmake`, which enabling the language
  in any directory loads, and the language is identified from that record. The record is held to
  the answer, because it can be a later configure's: one that identifies the compiler again -
  given another, or run with `--fresh` - rewrites it, and one that then fails writes no answer,
  which leaves the last one's beside a record of a compiler that built nothing there. Read that
  way, `test --no-build` named a compiler its binaries were not built with. So the record must name
  the compiler the answer names, where the answer names one; a record nothing ties to the answer
  identifies nothing, and the language is `unwitnessed`, with why. The answer keeps a toolchain
  file's value as written, where the record holds what CMake's
  `Modules/CMakeDetermineCompiler.cmake` made of it, so the two are compared as that: a list's
  first item - `gcc.exe;-m64` names `gcc.exe` - a path tidied of `.`, `..` and doubled separators,
  with forward slashes, and a name alone found as a program, with `.com` or `.exe` after it on
  Windows. Measured with CMake 3.29 and 4.3: MSVC through Ninja and through Visual Studio 18 2026,
  gcc on Windows and on Linux, toolchain files naming the compiler each of those ways, and a
  configure that failed after identifying the compiler again. Never by when either was written: a
  host whose clock steps forward for a moment stamps a file ahead of one written after it - on a
  consumer's WSL host, two files written a fraction of a second apart came out 24 seconds apart, and
  a configure's own record came out dated after its answer, failing a leg as `unwitnessed` - and a
  phase that starts and ends outside the step measures no drift. Read for the configure that wrote
  it, the record can be no later configure's: only what that configure answered is read, and nothing
  configures between it and the reading. Read for a directory a leg did not configure, a configure
  since is told apart by what CMake leaves of it: one that identified another program by the
  program the record names, and one that failed, whatever it identified, by the error index CMake 4
  writes in place of an answer - kept beside the last answer, where a configure that answers
  removes every one before it, measured with CMake 4.3. Before CMake 4 a configure that failed
  leaves nothing of itself there, and the record is read as it names it. A language
  CMake identified nowhere, such as the resource compiler it lists on Windows, is left out of the
  compilers, and a toolchain declaring one is told what CMake's answer named for it and why that
  is no id, never that CMake named none. `test --no-build` names what its build
  directory was last configured with, and holds it to the same `compilerId`: binaries a compiler
  nobody chose produced are failed rather than tested. A runner that does not build names none.
- **A compiler updated in place starts its build directory from clean.** CMake identifies a cached
  compiler once, when a build directory is first configured, and loads that record on every
  configure after; a build system has no edge on the compiler itself. A Visual Studio update
  rewrote `cl.exe`, `c1xx.dll` and `c2.dll` in the same toolset directory, taking `cl` from
  19.51.36257 to 19.51.36260, and a consumer's trees configured before it still recorded the old
  version: the first build of each failed every precompiled header with C1853, "from a different
  version of the compiler". So before each build of a CMake project, the C and C++ compilers the
  directory's records name - under the version of CMake that last answered there - are asked their
  versions as CMake identified them: a line naming the macros CMake's identification reads is
  preprocessed, in the leg's own environment, and the values put together by CMake's formula for the
  id it recorded - `_MSC_VER`, `_MSC_FULL_VER` and `_MSC_BUILD` for MSVC, `__GNUC__` with its minor and
  patch level for GNU, `__clang_major__` and its fellows for Clang, with `__apple_build_version__` for
  AppleClang. Never by which are defined: clang defines `__GNUC__` too, as 4.2.1. A version that
  differs, a compiler that is not there, or one that defines none of its id's macros starts the
  directory from clean, naming both versions. Preprocessing takes a fraction of a second, where a
  scratch configure took 19 with MSVC; measured against CMake 4.3's records, MSVC 19.51.36260.0
  through Visual Studio 18, MinGW gcc 13.2.0, Linux gcc 13.3.0 and clang 18.1.3 each came out as CMake
  wrote it. A compiler that cannot be asked is said and passed over - the question names the cause of
  a failure the build would show anyway - and one of another id is not asked.
- **A toolchain may name a developer environment**, declared once under `developerEnvironments`,
  and one naming none that is declared is refused, as is a `visualStudio` one on a toolchain whose
  `platforms` is not `["windows"]`: a leg elsewhere would be turned away on every run for want of it.
  `init`'s `msvc` toolchain names `visualStudio`. The survey asks every host a leg might land on
  whether it can set it up - Visual Studio's installer, `vswhere`, naming the newest instance with
  `requiresComponent` - and a host without one turns the leg away as `skipped-tool-missing`, naming
  why, one that could not look as `skipped-unavailable`, and one never asked as `poisoned`, a
  defect in this tool; a copy starts nothing and asks nothing. The host that runs the leg sets it up from the
  instance its own survey found, never a second look: that instance's `vcvarsall.bat` for the leg's
  processor (`amd64`, or `amd64_arm64` to cross-compile), run once per environment, instance,
  toolset, architecture and host environment by `cmd.exe` from a batch file the harness writes, reading
  `set` before and after it in UTF-16 and keeping only what changed; the batch file names its
  variables `%%NAME%%`, so only `call`'s own pass expands them, and a path holding `%`, `^` or `&`
  is used as it is. Its exit code, an `[ERROR` line in either encoding it prints, a
  `VSCMD_ARG_TGT_ARCH` naming another processor, an instance removed since the survey and a capture
  that cannot be written each fail the leg before anything of it starts: the survey found the
  instance, and an environment that will not set up once a leg began is that leg failing, as a
  program that will not start then is. A capture directory that cannot be removed afterwards is a
  warning and fails nothing. What it set sits over the host's `env` and beneath the variant's, the
  test invocation's and the runner's own, for every process the leg starts, so `cl` builds from a
  plain shell. The programs the leg starts - which no survey can require, since that `PATH` exists
  only once set up - are looked for on it then, before anything of the leg starts: one missing
  there skips the leg as `skipped-tool-missing`, named, never a program failing halfway through a
  build. Each leg's line names it - `developer environment: visualStudio (Visual Studio
  18.0.11205.157, MSVC 14.50.35717, amd64)` - and `--json` carries it as `developerEnvironment`,
  beside the detail rather than inside it, like the compilers.
- **A developer environment may hold its legs to one MSVC toolset**, with the optional
  `toolsVersion`: two numbers, naming the newest toolset of that line, or three, naming one, as
  `VC\Tools\MSVC` names its directories. Only that form is checked when the file is read - a blank
  one, one number, a side-by-side component's four (`14.44.17.14`, from which `vcvarsall.bat` falls
  back to another toolset with a warning) and anything else are refused - and nothing in the tool
  names a toolset: left out, `vcvarsall.bat` is given the architecture alone and sets up its
  instance's default. Named, the survey asks `vswhere -sort` for every instance with
  `requiresComponent`, newest first, and takes the first whose `VC\Tools\MSVC` holds a toolset it
  names, with the newest of those by their numbers (`VisualStudioToolsets`, the one owner of what a
  `toolsVersion` names); a host whose instances hold none turns the leg away as
  `skipped-tool-missing`, naming the toolset and what each instance holds, and one whose toolsets
  could not be listed as `skipped-unavailable`. The toolset found travels with the instance in the
  survey's answer, and the host that runs the leg runs `vcvarsall.bat` with `-vcvars_ver=` and
  exactly that toolset - never the shorter form, which `vcvarsall.bat` matches anywhere inside a
  directory's name, so `14.4` would take `14.44.35207` - and fails the leg where `VCToolsVersion`
  comes out as anything else. The leg's line names the MSVC set up. Two environments of one kind,
  one naming a toolset, keep two toolsets apart on one machine: a CUDA toolchain's legs on the
  toolset its `nvcc` accepts, every other MSVC leg on the instance's default.
- **A leg naming a toolchain that does not exist on its own operating system is refused**, by the
  toolchain's `platforms` list. Refused when read rather than skipped when placed, because nothing
  about it needs measuring: a leg's `os` is required, and a leg only ever runs on a host whose
  operating system equals it — emulation varies the processor, never the system. Skipping instead
  would also make the run report a leg that reached no verdict, which is not a success, so a wrong
  list would turn a green run non-zero rather than telling its author which line to fix. A
  project's `defaultToolchain` is held to the same rule, against the platform its key names, or
  against the operating systems its legs declare where the key is `all`.

It is written with LF line endings and no byte order mark on every platform. The file
is tracked, and its bytes must not depend on which machine ran `init`.

## Worktrees

`create-worktree` adds a worktree under the main checkout's `worktrees.root`, which defaults to
`.harness-config/worktrees`, and `delete-worktree` removes one, everything under it, and git's
record of it.

The root is configurable because it is spent before a worktree's own name. The default costs 25
characters of the Windows path budget, and a repository whose build paths are long has no name left
that fits; a shorter root such as `.worktrees` buys those characters back. The budget is still
checked against the real path, so a shorter root never hides an overrun — it only makes one
avoidable. What lies below a worktree is reckoned by one owner, `WorktreeRoom`, which a run's
start asks too, so a run that passed its start never fails on a worktree it needs: the deeper of
the longest file the repository tracks at the main checkout's HEAD, where every worktree is made,
and - where a leg builds on this machine - `build/<variant>` for the longest variant with
`worktrees.pathBudgetReserve` below it; where no leg builds here, the reserve guesses at nothing
and is not counted. Every build measures the deepest path it left below its build directory against the
reserve, and warns where it went deeper. A Ninja build leaves out of that the outputs ninja says no
target of the current build produces any more - asked as a dry run of `ninja -t cleandead`, which
names them and removes nothing - since a new worktree's build directory, starting from clean, never
holds them; it notes them instead, where one is deeper than the reserve, naming the command that
removes them. A consumer's incremental builds warned every time about the object of a test renamed
away. `ninja -t query` would not have told it apart - ninja's dependency log still knows the path -
and what CMake's configure writes is no output of the manifest at all. A leftover ninja does not
