Merging two changes of one file is git's work, never a comparison of lines made here (`GitClient.Merge.cs`). Each of
the three versions - what both held, and each side's - is first read as git would store it at the path
(`IGitClient.ReadStagedAsync`), as `git add` would record it there: a blob as it is, and a file or bytes in hand as
the file at the path would be (`git hash-object -w --path=<path>` run at the work tree's root, then `cat-file
--batch`). The path's clean filters run from the root, as git add runs them, and its attributes and line-ending rules
apply: a file one tree checked out with other line endings merges as `git merge` would merge it, and one committed
with carriage returns, under `core.autocrlf` or a `text=auto` attribute, keeps them on every side, as git keeps them,
so a merge git makes clean is clean. git stores a file to read it so, and what it stores goes to an object directory
of the question's own - a temporary directory as `GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY`, the repository's own as
`GIT_ALTERNATE_OBJECT_DIRECTORIES`, quoted so a path holding the character that parts that list is still one entry -
discarded with the answer: neither the repository's objects nor its index are written by a merge that was only
measured. What git would record for a file is asked in one place (`GitClient.StoredIdsAsync`), of `hash-object` at the
work tree's root, told the two things `git add` reads in the index and hash-object does not (`GitClient.StoringAsync`).
Where `git ls-files --eol` says the path's entry holds carriage returns (`i/crlf`, `i/mixed`) and its line endings are
converted only as git sees fit (no attribute under `core.autocrlf`, or `text=auto`), git leaves that conversion out,
and hash-object is told to as well: `core.autocrlf` off; the bytes as they stand, where nothing else converts the
file; or, where a clean filter, `ident` or `working-tree-encoding` still does, the path's attributes declared whole
with `text` unset, in a tree of the question's own git reads attributes from instead (`--attr-source`, git 2.41's). A
path below an attribute file the work tree lacks, which git reads from the index, has its attributes declared so too.
An older git, which refuses that option as unknown and has no other way to be told, is refused before it is asked
anything for the file, naming git 2.41 and the version installed, which is asked of git once
(`GitClient.InstalledVersionAsync`). info/attributes outranks that tree: where it says otherwise of the path, the question is refused, said, never guessed.
Nothing is staged, so no index is written and no mark on an entry stands for a file's bytes; every index the tool does
write of its own is written with `core.ignoreStat` off, in one place (`GitClient.RunCoreAsync`), so no comparison made
with it reads an edited file as its entry's blob. `GitClient.HashAsync` is the one caller of `hash-object`, told what
differs - written or not, filtered or not, as which path, what git is told first, into which directory.
The three are brought to the form git stores, unpacked by git into files (`UnpackedAsync`) and
merged there by `git merge-file -p --diff3` (`MergeAsync`), outside any repository, so a file of
any size merges as a small one does and never passes through memory; the merged text is kept as a
blob in the repository's objects and reaches each tree only as a checkout of it writes it
(`CheckedOutAsync`). Its exit code says whether it merged: 0 is a clean merge; one from 1 is a
merge with conflicts, counted by their markers in what it wrote, for git's code stops at 127;
anything else is no merge - a binary file, for one - kept in git's own words. `--diff3` is passed
so no configuration changes what a conflict shows, and the markers are
made one longer than the longest line of the three that could be read as one, so a file that holds such lines is
merged like any other. Every conflict is shown whole, every line of every one: the command line
gives them whole, and an agent reads them a page at a time by the call's id (`read_result`). How
many hunks each side brought is git's count too (`git diff --no-index -U0` of each side against
what both held). The merged bytes are brought to what a checkout would write (`ReadCheckedOutAsync`: `cat-file
--filters --path=<path>`) and written as a copy between trees is - beside the destination, read back, compared by
SHA-256, put in place in one step (`VerifiedFileCopy.WriteAsync`) - with the execute bit asked for
(`IFilePermissions.SetExecutable`, which changes nothing on Windows, where no such bit is kept), not the bit of the
file replaced. What a history held at a path is asked with `git rev-list --full-history` (`ListHeldInHistoryAsync`),
since a version a merge dropped was still that history's, for one more commit than its bound, which is how a history
cut short is told from one read whole, its paths taken literally (`--literal-pathspecs`), so `[id].tsx` is that file
and never a pattern; and what git's attributes declare for a path is asked of `git check-attr`
(`ReadAttributesAsync`), by this and by fix-line-endings alike, whose refusal where git cannot answer reads as it
always has: `git check-attr failed, so the declared policy could not be read and nothing was rewritten: <git's
words>`. Every answer read as bytes - a blob, a merge, a checkout, a listing of names - is decoded from its first byte
under the encoding asked for (`ProcessRunner`): bytes that begin as a byte order mark does are the file's, or the
name's, never taken to say how the rest is written.

rebase-agent moves an agent's base to the main tree's HEAD (`AgentFold.MeasureRebaseAsync`). Each path the two commits
hold differently (`git diff --name-only`, commit to commit) is shared - kept as its seed records it, since the seed,
not the base, is what a shared path is weighed against - or held as the new base holds it already, or held as the old
base holds it, and comes in as git holds it (`git checkout --no-overlay <commit>`, the paths on standard input and read
literally), or changed by the agent - asked of git against both commits, with anything where the old base holds
nothing its own, untracked, ignored or staged - which refuses the move unless `--settled` names it. A file the agent
changed that the main tree committed a change to is two changes of one file, resolved where a fold resolves one
(`TwoChanges`): what both held is the old base's blob, ours the new base's, theirs the agent's file, merged in the
agent's worktree's forms, and the bit from the two bases' entries and the agent's file (`ListEntriesAtAsync`, which says
too where a base holds a link). A link among the versions - a base's entry, or the agent's file where it is one or is
reached through one along its path (`LinkPaths.LeadsElsewhere`), its directory turned into a link - is offered no merge,
decided where a fold's is (`TwoChanges.OfferAsync`, from `TwoChangeSide.Link` and `TwoChangeAncestor.Committed.Link`),
so nothing is read or written through it. Its refusal says what the merge gives and names the command
that takes the clean ones; `--merge` takes one, listed before what comes in, written over the agent's file as weighed
(`AgentFold.WriteMergeAsync`, the one writer of a merge) once git has written the rest and before HEAD moves, and
recorded nowhere: on the new base it is the agent's own change, which its fold weighs. A `--merge` naming a path the two
commits hold alike is refused as a misspelling, and one naming any other path they changed is let stand, so the command
that finishes a stopped move runs again; a path named with both `--merge` and `--settled` is a usage error, exit 10. The arm registry is merged by arm as a fold merges it (below): what both
held is the old base's blob as git stores it, or nothing where the agent made the registry the new base brings; ours is
the new base's blob as a checkout into the agent's worktree writes it (`CommittedBytes.CheckedOutAsync`, the one reader
of a commit's blob in that form, which `TreeAfter.Moved` reads through too), so the merge ends its
lines as that checkout would; and the merged text is judged by the worktree as the move leaves it, each path the move
takes read from its blob when the validation asks for it (`TreeAfter.Moved`). One thing the agent
made is not its change: a file that is the very file the new base holds there, which is held as the new base holds it
already (`IGitClient.ListHeldAsAtAsync`: the new base's entry for each such file put in an index of the question's own,
and `git diff` asked against it, so the content is compared through the clean filters and the line-ending rules and the
mode where the repository trusts one, as status will compare them once the index has moved - whatever the worktree's
own index says of the path, nothing for an untracked file). What each commit holds at a path is told apart (`HeldAtAsync`): a directory the old base
held, now a file or a submodule's entry, is held as the old base holds it while the agent's worktree holds a directory
or nothing there, and a submodule's entry as git compares it, so neither is taken for something the agent made.
Nothing of the agent's is written over or hidden: git removes a file or a link where a path it writes needs a
directory, removes a directory, with all it holds, where it writes a file, and hides all a directory holds where it
writes a submodule's entry the old base did not hold - a submodule's own checkout it leaves alone - so each refuses the
move unless it is the old base's own, coming in with the rest - the agent's own, settled or shared, each named with
what to do. A file or a submodule's entry where the old base held a directory is written last
(`RebasePlan.WrittenLast`), once what was below it is: written first, git removes that, with the directories it leaves
empty, where asked for both at once it finds that gone and stops, and a submodule's entry written first leaves it in
place, hidden from git. Where the worktree's file system finds a name in any case, a file the new base renamed in case
alone is that one file (`AgentFold.RenamedInCase`): what the worktree holds at the new name is the file at the old one,
never a file the agent made there, and the new name is written last, once the old is removed - written first, the
removal of the old name would take it. It comes in only with its old name: where the agent keeps what it holds there -
declared settled, shared with the main tree, or its own change - the new name refuses the move, naming both, since
writing it would write over that; a shared file the agent changed is to be folded first, since no refresh hands a path
the agent changed, and one it did not to be refreshed under the new name, which records the file it holds as shared
there. Where it holds nothing at the old name, the new name refuses the move as a rename and a deletion of one file -
its old name to be put back with `git checkout HEAD` and the move run again, the new name deleted after only where the
agent's session deleted the old, or, shared, never taken by a move and so the agent's deletion, folded and committed in
the main tree - unless the move being finished removed it, the new name written last, as its record says
(`MovingRemoved`: the old names the agent's index no longer holds once the git checking out what the move writes first
ends, having written it all or stopped part way). git leaves the index and the disk alike after that checkout and after
a `git rm` of the agent's session; a removal of the move's its record missed - a move killed between git and its
record - is refused so, costing a refusal, never a file. The main checkout keeps the commit the move goes to alive
(`refs/harness/worktree-moving/<orchestrator>/<agent>`, exit 20 and nothing changed where it cannot) and the record
names where the move goes (`Moving`) before anything is written; then each
path the move takes is asked to hold what was measured there (`RebasePlan.Held`, `AgentFold.RequireTakenAsync`), so a
file the agent's session wrote since stops the move, exit 21, before git writes anything, never written over; then the new
base's paths are written, HEAD and the index move (`git reset --mixed`), then the record and the worktree's base ref
name the new base, and the move's keepalive goes: a move that stopped part way, exit 21, is finished where it was going by running rebase-agent
again - the command its last words name, with every `--merge` and `--settled` the move was given, a merge it wrote
merged again to the same bytes - whatever the main tree committed since, and with what it wrote held as the new base holds it, a file the old
base lacked included - and fold-agent, delete-agent, seed-agent and refresh-agent refuse the agent until then, naming
that same command, which the record keeps beside where the move goes (`MovingWith`). Only a move its record names is ever finished, and only from its base or where it goes: a HEAD anywhere else was
moved by hand - back, forward or beside its base, a move under way or not - or names no commit, and each command
refuses it, saying how to put it back; one past its base that the main tree's history does not hold is a commit made
inside the agent. Where git cannot say which a HEAD is, each fails, exit 20, saying so, never guessing.

An agent's contribution is a measurement (`AgentFold`): its worktree's status, and every path it shares with the
main tree whether its status lists it or not, less the shared paths left as they were. Each path goes in exactly one
list - its own, deleted, inherited, already in the main tree, merged, settled - or is refused, and one refusal refuses the whole
fold before anything is written. A shared path is compared with what both trees held - a file, or its absence; any
other with the blob at the agent's own base (`cat-file --batch-check`, one process), never the main tree's HEAD, which a
sibling's committed fold moves, and the main tree is asked whether it moved from that base as git status would answer
(`git diff --name-only` against the base, one process): through the index's line-ending rules, so a file only checked
out with other line endings is no change, and with its mode, so a sibling's changed execute bit is one. A fold records
what it wrote, removed and found already in as shared - each at what the agent's worktree held when it was measured,
the file whole with its bit, so a bit its session changes after the weighing is the agent's own change to fold, never
silently absorbed - so a later fold - after a review sends the agent back - weighs
those paths against what the fold left, never against the base: the agent putting a path back as it was is its change
to fold. A refusal of a main-tree path the agent shares nothing for, made, changed, made a directory of or removed since
the agent's base, says whether a commit, an uncommitted edit or a commit and then an edit did it, since each is
reconciled differently: a commit alone where the main tree's HEAD already holds what the main tree holds there now,
which `git status` - untracked files listed, its paths compared in any case where the main tree's file system finds a
name in any case, so a rename of case alone is the commit's - answers by listing nothing at the path, below it, or in a
directory above it that it folds into one
entry, as it folds an untracked repository nested in the tree (one process a fold, asked only where a commit moved a
path or neither HEAD nor the base holds one); an uncommitted edit alone where HEAD holds what the base holds, each entry
compared as git compares a commit, so a commit of a mode alone is a commit; and both otherwise, each said with what it
did - the edit after what the commit did where the edit made what the main tree holds of another kind than HEAD's, and
the commit then the edit's change where the commit already made it of that kind. A file of the main tree in the way of
the agent's - where one of its files needs a directory, or in a directory one replaces - is a file the fold does not
remove, said made or changed since the base where the main tree did either, the same way, and a file git ignores
where neither HEAD nor the base holds one - as `git check-ignore` says, asked only of what status lists nothing at
where HEAD holds nothing and no submodule holds the path, never read from what status leaves out - is said ignored by
git, with no word of when it came. A file of a submodule of the main tree's in the way - below a gitlink its index
holds, where git looks at nothing and `check-ignore` answers nothing - came as that record did: by a commit where HEAD
holds it, then changed by an uncommitted edit where status lists the record, and by an uncommitted edit where only the
index holds it (`Came`, the one wording of how a path came to be held, and `Since`, of what the main tree did, both
decided once). The base's entry and HEAD's are found alike, as git spells the path and, where the main tree's file
system finds a name in any case, in any case, whatever `core.ignorecase` says, so a rename of case alone is the
commit's that made it, and none other's. Each tree's status is read alike: where `core.ignorecase` says the
repository heeds case, an untracked name the index holds under another spelling is dropped only where every
directory the two spell differently lists the untracked spelling alone, finds it in another case it does not list,
and reaches something by the index's spelling, and the part they spell differently is ASCII - decided file by file,
as each directory compares names, since a tree may hold a directory that tells names apart below one that does not
(`GitClient.IndexedInAnotherCaseAsync`, read by the one status question and by `check-root-litter`). So a file the
disk spells otherwise than the index - as a write put in place over it leaves it on macOS, which keeps the old
spelling where Windows takes the new - is one file, never changed under one name and untracked under the other,
while a new file beside a tracked one a directory tells apart, or beside a tracked one deleted, stays listed. Left as
it is: where the part spelled otherwise holds a character outside ASCII, the name is kept, on every system - a disk
may hold it composed otherwise in Unicode than git gives it, and the invariant culture this build reads names in
composes nothing - so with `core.ignorecase` false such a file is listed under both spellings, a fold of it stops
part way at the second, and `check-root-litter` names it. git is never told to ignore case: that would match the
repository's ignore rules in any case too, and hide a new file they do not ignore as it spells them. Whether a
directory finds a name in any case is asked of the directory itself, by a name it holds in another case
(`PathCase.In`): one made case-sensitive under folders that are not compares exactly. A shared path's
refusal says the main tree changed it after the agent was last handed it or folded, which the seed records alike. A deletion needs the same baseline proof a copy does. A directory with no `.git` of its own
holds no file at its path, so a file the agent turned into a directory folds as the file's deletion and the directory's
files, and a directory it turned into a file as the files' deletions and the file: every removal is made first, with
the directories it empties, then every file written. A path reached through a link in either tree, a repository of
its own - a submodule, or the agent's own - a path in a submodule of the main tree's - at or below a gitlink its index
holds, said made by a commit or staged by an uncommitted edit, and left out where settled by hand, since nothing a fold
wrote there could be committed in the main tree - what the main tree holds in the way of the agent's files (a file
where one needs a directory, or files the fold does not remove in a directory one replaces), a HEAD off the base and a move of
the base stopped part way are refused, and so is an anchor registry the agent changed as a file: its rows go in through its rows directory, weighed
against the registry the fold would otherwise have written over. `--settled` is the way out of any path's refusal -
`--merge` only of a path whose merge is clean - and a deletion can be settled too; a settled path the fold does not
weigh is refused as a misspelling. So is a `--merge`
naming no path the fold weighs, while one naming a path it weighs with nothing left to merge is let stand, so the
command line of a fold that stopped part way runs again. A path named with both `--merge` and `--settled` is a usage
error, exit 10, before anything is read, and a `--merge` naming an anchor registry or the arm registry is refused. A path the main
tree already holds as the agent does is already in, so a fold run again finds its own writes. Where the agent's
worktree finds a name in any case, two paths it changes that differ in case alone are one file there; where its git
index spells that file otherwise than its base does, found in any case, the agent renamed it in case alone, and
each path is read only where a tree spells the file so (`AgentFold.Spellings`) - as its git index does, where it holds
the file under one spelling, since a rename git makes in the index alone leaves a directory's name on disk as it was,
and otherwise as its file system does (`PathCase.Spelled`) - never as the other. Where the main tree's git index spells
that file otherwise, each tree holding it, and the main tree finds a name in any case too, a fold cannot
write the rename - the main tree's git would go on naming the file as before - so it is refused by name, saying to run
`git mv -f` there, forced since git finds the new name taken where the repository does not say it ignores case; once
that is run, the old name is already in, absent from both. Every path the agent shares nothing for is weighed against
the base's entry found as git spells it, as `Came` finds it, so a file renamed in case alone is weighed against the
base's under its old name: an edit made with the rename merges with the main tree's, and a removal of the file in the
main tree refuses it, never undone. A path this process
cannot look at is never read as absent, which would take the agent's file for its deletion: the fold fails before
anything is written. A file of either tree that changed after it was weighed is never written over: the agent's copy is
refused where it no longer holds the SHA-256 weighed (`VerifiedFileCopy`), and the main tree's file is weighed again
before each write and each removal. The fold stops there, exit 21, for a run again to weigh it anew.

A path named with `--settled` was reconciled in the main tree by hand, and the fold acts on it (`AgentFold.MeasureAsync`,
in this order): one leading out of the main tree is refused, as any is; one reached through a link in either tree, or a
directory git will not look into in either, is left out and said to be (`FoldPlan.LeftOut`), since a fold never reads
or writes it; one both trees and the seed agree on is inherited, so the line that ran once runs again; one the two
trees hold alike is already in, and recorded; one where the main tree holds other than what the agent last shared - or,
for a path it shares nothing for, than its base - is handed (`FoldPlan.Handed`); and one only the agent changed is
refused, since nothing was reconciled there and handing the main tree's copy would undo its work. What is handed is
sorted as any hand-over sorts what the main tree holds, asked what of the agent's own it would go over or through
(`InTheWayOfHanding`), and measured in the agent's worktree; `ApplyAsync` hands it last, after every write of the main
tree, through the one loop every hand-over takes - deletions, then files, each asked first to be what was weighed - and
`FoldedAsync` records it through the ledger. Every write the engine makes in the main tree - a fold's apply, a
deletion's, a refresh's and a rebase's apply, a commit step - takes the main tree's lock (`MainTreeWriteLock`, a
`MachineWideMutex` named for the tree's path) once, before the measure its write is held to, and keeps that one hold to
its last write - a commit step from its first read of the main tree's git through its commit's own check - which a
side-task's writes and commands take for their duration too, the graph tool's edit among them, never its reads: each
side waits the other out, for a long command holds the folds back for as long as it runs, so nothing the engine weighed
is changed under it before it writes, and the step's output says how long it waited and for what
(`MainTreeWriteLock.WaitedFor`). The command's or the step's own stop ends the engine's wait, nothing weighed or
written. A fold, and a deletion that folds, called by a step of a run, record in the run's ledger of its folds, under
that hold and before they let it go, that their write begins and then what it left at each path - through the
`FoldIntent` their request carries (`FoldLedger.Writing`, `FoldLedger.WrittenAsync`), also where the write throws part
way; a deletion lets the hold go before its transcripts, its evidence and its worktree's removal. So whatever comes after -
the verb's answer, a throw, a crash, a side-task's write let in once the hold is let go - the ledger settles the fold by
what it recorded, never by the tree after; from the command line there is no ledger and nothing is recorded. The one
limit is a fold that dies inside its own hold, part way through its write: the next attempt reads what it left from the
tree, under the lock as well, and marks it so, for a side-task's write made between the death and that read cannot be
told from the fold's. Every intent the ledger writes says that its verb records its write (`FlowFoldEntry.RecordsWrite`);
an intent left unsettled that does not say so - an earlier release's, whose verb recorded nothing of its write and may
have written all of it - is read from the tree in the same way, never settled as found.
On Claude Code the lock is taken where it is on the API clients: by the tool runtime, as the
engine's tool server runs the call (`AgentToolRuntime.ServeAsync`).
A lock that cannot be taken denies the call with its refusal on every
client (`MainTreeWriteLock.Refusal`), recorded as every denial is, the run going on; the
side-task's policy refuses, on every client, a command that leaves a process running
after it ends (`MainTreeWriteLock.LeftBehind`), asked of each command where its rules are (`AgentPolicy.RunDecided`), so
a script a shell runs and one the string wrote and then runs meet it as the string's own commands do: one the command
reader reads as run in the background (`AnalyzedCommand.Background`) - a lone `&` ends its list, never `&&`, a
redirect's `&` or a quoted one, nor cmd's, which runs the next command in turn and is read as `;`; a `coproc`'s
command; a process substitution's body, `<(...)` or `>(...)`, which the shell does not wait for whatever its command
reads; PowerShell's job `&`; or one run by a program that keeps what it starts apart
(`CommandAnalysis.Detaching`) wherever a program of the command runs (`CommandAnalysis.RunsAt`) - a program by the
last segment of any path to it, the shells' and PowerShell's own commands - `start`, `Start-Process`, `Start-Job`,
`disown` and their kin - by the bare word alone, so `./bin/start` and `scripts\start` are the repository's scripts, and
where PowerShell reads the command (`CommandAnalysis.ReadBy`, the innermost shell that runs it) its cmdlets by a
module-qualified name too (`Microsoft.PowerShell.Management\Start-Process`) - or one PowerShell reads given `-AsJob`,
never another program's `-as` cluster - which a contained `run_command`'s end would not reach either where it leaves
the session. A terminal session's program given what to run, `systemd-run`, and a `start` or `Start-Process`
told to wait, which hands its program a command line of its own, are refused to every agent before the lock weighs
them. The refusal is of what the command names: what a program detaches by itself - a dev server's own daemon mode, an
interpreter's code - is not read, the OS layer standing behind the words. Holding the lock until the command's process
group is gone was rejected: the client never sees a detached command's end, only the result it is handed.
While a run's owner is live
(`.orchestrators/<run>.owner.json`, asked at each call through `AgentPolicyGround.LiveRun`), a side-task's agent is
refused, with the run's name, every command that writes the git state the run works over (`AgentPolicy.LiveRunHeld`:
git's state-writing verbs, the verbs that write its index and gh's that write git's state, each whole, and beside them
`AgentPolicy.GitStateForms`, a fetch's `--update-head-ok` wherever it stands, an expansion held as one that may be it
where it may give it - beginning its word, after a start the option may have, or unquoted, which the shell may split -
and the refusal of one only an unquoted expansion makes so saying that quoting it lets it through,
`AgentPolicy.QuoteTheExpansion`) - met as the worktree rules meet a command,
by every reading `CommandAnalysis.ForRules` gives it and with a verb the shell expands held as one that may be any, their
forms that only read open: those a verb decides as patterns (`AgentPolicy.LiveRunOpen`), and git branch, tag, config,
symbolic-ref, reflog and notes in a mode that only reads, read as git reads their options wherever they stand
(`CommandAnalysis.GitReadsOnly`, over the getopt reader and each verb's option table; an option it does not know, a
word the shell expands among their words and the reading made of a configuration set where the command runs
(`RuleReading.Configures`) held) - a run that starts while the chat is open is held to
from its first step, and one that ends releases it - and the run's
own verbs and the agent verbs are refused it always, as every verb that writes the tool's state is. Both trees and the seed then agree, so the agent's next fold starts from
the reconciliation, and delete-agent's proof that nothing is left to fold holds without being told which paths were
settled. rebase-agent's `--settled` is another option: there the person reconciled the agent's copy, which stays as its
change on the new base.

A side-task may use the codebase graph beside all this, unlimited: a graph of its own under its records
(`SideTaskGraph`), held in the one shape every graph's records take, seeded from the newest the repository holds - a
run's or another side-task's - at its opening, then incremental and synced after each of its agent's writes and
commands on either client (`AfterWrites`), the tool answering from what each sync leaves; the `graph` tool offered
among its agent's own with every operation, `edit` among them, on every client, and no narrowing, what it reads and an edit writes asked of the side-task's own policy.
Pull, not push, as for a step at `tools`: nothing of the graph is pushed - every message reaches the agent as the person
typed it, on every client and in either shape, a line posted to a launch Claude Code holds open for a chat among them -
and the repository map (`CodebaseRepositoryMap`), made once at its opening, and the context pack made from each message
(`SideTaskGraph.MakePack`, which either shape calls before the message goes) are the pages the tool's `map` and `pack`
give from page 1, offered by the steps' one rule (`CodebaseGraphTool.Operations`), the last message's pack's `Near`
breaking `find`'s ties; `--no-graph` turns it off, and a graph that cannot be made takes nothing from the conversation: the side-task says once that it runs
without one and why - the chat's first line, or a line beside a one shot's records - and its `graph.jsonl` holds the
prompt line naming why no pack is given (`GraphPromptLine.Why`).

A path both trees changed - each holds a file there, neither is what the two last agreed on, and they differ - is
resolved in one place, whichever command meets it (`TwoChanges`, made for each command with that command's
`TwoChangePolicy`: the arm registry's path, the anchor registries' and the paths named with `--merge`). Every such
path is weighed in full before anything is written, asked for or not, and what a three-way merge of it gives ends
the path's refusal: clean, with the hunks each side brought; conflicting, with the conflicts shown under the
refusals; or none offered, with why - one of a closed list (`NoMerge`) that owns each reason's sentence, so no
command words one itself. The refusal then names the command that takes the clean ones. Asking, `--merge <path>`
once for each, changes one thing: a clean merge is taken. None is offered for a deletion against a change, a path
both trees made with nothing either held there before, a version that is a link or is reached through one, one whose
`merge` attribute asks for another merge than git's own of text, or one git
reads as binary or will not merge - a file of any size merges as a small one does; and an anchor registry, which changes only through the rows an agent files, and the arm
registry are never merged by line. The arm registry - the configured `mutations.registry` - is merged by arm instead,
with no option given (`TwoChangeRule.Arms`): its three versions go to `MutationRegistryMerge.Merge` as the bytes each
tree holds, nothing staged and nothing git merges, so the merge ends its lines as the main tree's file does; what both
held is found as for any path, and is nothing only where neither tree held a registry before - shared bytes that cannot
be found offer no merge, since a merge from nothing takes an arm one side removed for the other's addition. A clean
merge is taken only once its text (`Merged.Text`) reads as a registry of the tree the command leaves
(`TwoChanges.JudgedAsync`, through `MutationRegistryValidation.ValidateAsync` with the configuration the command
loaded): `TreeAfter` makes that tree an `OverlaidRegistryFiles` over `TreeRegistryFiles.OfAsync` of the tree the
registry is written into, each path the command writes there read only when the validation asks for it - a fold's from
the agent's files, its merges from the bytes in hand, and what it removes gone - so a fold of hundreds of paths reads the
few the registry cites. Arms the two changed differently (`ArmConflict`, shown under the refusals), a version that cannot
be read as a registry, and a merged text that does not read as one - every problem listed as `check-mutations` words it,
`as the fold would write it` - refuse the path, and `--merge` naming the registry is refused: it is never merged by line.
Run again after a fold that wrote it into one tree only, the merge of its own result gives that result again. What both held is, for a path the agent shares, the bytes kept under the digest
its seed records, used only where they still hash to it; where the seed was written by a build that kept none, the
versions of the path in the main tree's history are read (`ListHeldInHistoryAsync`, its whole
history read once by git's own walk, each blob it held compared once, a batch at a time by size), each as its commit holds it and then as a checkout writes it, and the first that hashes
to the recorded digest is taken - kept by a fold that goes on to write, so it is looked for once, and never by a dry
run. A version git cannot check out - a filter that fails on it - is passed over and said with the rest: the path is
offered no merge, and nothing else of the fold depends on it. For any other path it is the blob at the agent's base. Nothing is merged against a guess: where neither gives
it, no merge is offered, and the line says why. A fold merges in the main tree's forms, since the same bytes go to
both trees and one digest is then true of both. Whether a file can be run is merged with its content
(`TwoChanges.MergedBit`): the merged bit is the one that differs from what both held, where either side's does. A
bit has two values, so two sides that both changed it changed it alike, and it never conflicts by itself - where
something was held before: a registry both trees made, merged by arm from nothing, whose two copies differ in the bit
is offered no merge (`NoMerge.BitBothMade`), since with nothing before neither bit is a change. What both
held is the seed's record of the bit for a shared path - whichever source gave the bytes, since a kept copy is bytes
under a digest and holds no bit - and the base's entry for any other (`ListEntriesAtAsync`, for those paths alone);
each side's is its file's. Where the platform keeps no such bit, as on Windows, none is read, merged or set. A merged
path is written after the fold's own writes: both trees' copies are asked to be what was weighed - the content, and
the bit where the platform keeps one (`MergedPath.Into`, each `MergeTarget` with what it was when weighed) - before either is written, the main tree's is written first, and the path is recorded as shared, at the merged bytes and bit, only once
both hold it. Stopped between the two, the main tree holds the merge, the agent its own copy and the seed what both
held before; the same command run again merges those again, and since every change of the agent's is already in the
merge, comes to the same bytes. A tree that already holds what the merge gives is not written again.

The rows an agent files (`AgentRows`) are read strictly - a directory for each anchor, a file for each cell, read
as write-anchor reads a cell file - and applied through `IAnchorRegistryService.ApplyAsync`, which composes each
row exactly as write-anchor or set-anchor does, one after another under the registries' one lock: every row is
checked and every refusal named before any is written, a row already as declared is left alone, a change names
only the cells that differ, a row moving between the registries is written destination first, and a write that
fails, or rows that do not read back as declared, put both registries back byte for byte. Every write of a row, alone
or in a batch, is held to what writing a row is (below). A batch makes a row no registry holds only where the request
names it new (`--new` of fold-agent and delete-agent), as write-anchor is only ever asked to make one, and writes a cell
whose stored text does not survive word for word - neither respaced, nor kept whole in an addendum, nor filling an
empty one (`AnchorCellComparison`) - only where the request accepts it (`--accept-lost`); a plan
(`AnchorBatchMode.Plan`, the dry run) shows such a cell word by word, and a check or an apply refuses it, so a fold
refuses before its files are written. Every refusal of a row is collected, so one run names them all. The directories a
fold makes at the top of the tree are handed to the batch (`AnchorBatchRequest.Roots`), so its rows are judged the same
before its files are written and after. The rows a fold applied are recorded as declared
then (`applied-rows.json`), and every row the agent declares is sent with that record (`AnchorBatchRequest.Earlier`):
one it declares as it did then is `Untouched` - never judged, never written, and not among the rows the batch's
others may cite - so a change the registries took since, the orchestrator closing the row or a sibling's
cross-reference, stands. One it declares anew over it is weighed cell by cell inside `ApplyAsync`, under the lock its
write takes, so it is decided against the registries as they are written (`AnchorCellMerge`): each of its five cells -
priority, status, trigger, closing, cross-refs - three ways, the earlier declaration the ancestor. A cell only the
agent changed is written; one only the registries changed is kept, said, and kept again at each fold until the agent
changes it, since the record stays the declaration rather than what the registries held - recording theirs would make
the agent's unchanged file read as its change; one both changed alike is left; one both changed otherwise is shown
with its three texts and written only where `--accept-over` names it, which consents too to what the registries'
text loses. The verdict is one decision, and `AnchorCellMerge` alone weighs it so, given the anchor settings: where
`anchors.triggerCarriesVerdict` holds, a row's status and trigger state its verdict together
(`AnchorCellMerge.VerdictCells`), so where the registries changed one of the two and the agent the other - one kept,
the other the agent's alone or both changed - and the row merged cell by cell would state two verdicts
(`AnchorStatus.SplitVerdict`) though the agent's declaration states one, both are `Both`, each carrying the two
verdicts it resolves (`AnchorCellWeighed.Verdict`, `AnchorOverCell.Verdict`) so the dry run's line and the refusal say
why a cell one side never changed asks for a consent. Named, the agent's two are written together and the row moves as
set-anchor would move it: a row the orchestrator reopened that the agent closes again with its trigger, its status file
closed as it was, goes back to the done registry, and its mirror, a row the orchestrator closed that the agent keeps
open, to the pending one. Until both are named nothing of the row is written, so the registries' verdict stands and no
row of two verdicts is ever written; a fold step of a run asks for them as for any cell both changed. A declaration
that states two verdicts itself is no one decision to take: the row is refused for the two verdicts before any cell
of it is weighed - whatever the row taken one from each side would state, which may agree by chance - with no
consent asked that could not mend it. Where the setting does not hold, the trigger carries no
verdict and the status alone states it, weighed as any cell is: a status the agent's file holds as it declared it at
its earlier fold is no decision of the agent's, so the registries' change of it is kept, whatever the agent's trigger
says, and an `--accept-over` naming it is refused as naming a cell not both changed. The row the registries are to hold (`AnchorRowOutcome.Effective`) is composed and judged by the same code
as any change, so every rule about a status, a closure or a move between the registries judges it, and the rows read
back are compared with it, not with what was declared. A declared cell is compared with a stored one through one
`AnchorRowCells`, as a row stores it. A row an earlier fold applied that the registries no longer hold is refused, to
be set by hand. The fold never writes the agent's row files: its report tells the agent, once, to write the
registries' text into a kept cell's file before it changes it.

### Deleting an agent

delete-agent measures everything first, under the run lock on the main tree and on the agent's worktree: the
fold and the rows, or with `--discard-uncommitted` what the agent changed. It writes the fold and the rows, proves
nothing is left to fold - the removal's discard of uncommitted work is built from that measurement alone - copies
the agent's Claude transcripts by session id (`ClaudeTranscripts`; found by file name alone, since Claude Code's
format is its own; one not found is said, and one found and not kept stops the deletion before the agent is
closed), and keeps the evidence roots' files, over the roots named before the fold and after it, in the agent's
directory, in a directory named for the run, every copy proved as it is made (`AgentEvidence`, which finds files as a
removal reaches them through `WorktreeEvidence`, the walk delete-worktree's evidence check makes: never through a link,
and a root that is or passes through one, and a link under one, neither kept nor counted). Only then does it record the agent closed: which git worktree it was
(`WorktreeStamp`, the creation and write times of `commondir` in its git directory, which a new worktree at the
same path does not share) and every path it held with its digest. It deletes the evidence originals still holding
what was kept - one that cannot be deleted is named and left, and stops the removal - and asks delete-worktree for
the removal - never forced, its evidence check kept, so a file written after the copy was read back stops it rather
than going with it - then proves the removal: directory gone, git's record gone, no copy recorded on a host. A
question it cannot answer is named as that, never read as nothing left. Once its record says it is deleted, the bytes
kept of what it shared go (`SharedCopies.Remove`): nothing merges from them any more, and they are not evidence, so
delete-orchestrator asks no `--delete-evidence` for them; where they cannot be removed a line says so, and the
deletion stands. An agent made under a worktrees root the
configuration no longer names is refused with nothing touched, since delete-worktree looks under the root the
configuration names.

A closed agent is never folded, seeded or refreshed again. delete-agent run again compares its worktree with what
closing recorded, never with the main tree, which later agents go on changing: a file changed or new since is
work, left for a person (exit 21); a file gone since is the debris of a removal that stopped part way; a path the
main tree ignores is never work, asked of the main tree with its index, since the removal may have deleted the
worktree's own ignore rules first. A directory with no `.git` of its own is never read - git would answer for the
main checkout - and never forced: its evidence is kept again, and the forced removal is named for a person. A
worktree made at the path since is another, and not the agent's to remove.

## Workflow definitions

A workflow is a flow of typed steps that depend on one another by name, declared by name under
`workflows` in `config.json` and defined by a yml file of its own,
`.harness-config/workflows/<name>/<name>.yml` - never an entry in the configuration, which holds the
names and nothing else. The workflow's directory is the workflow's own - its agent files
(`agents/<name>.md`), its prompts, its schemas, the bar it recommends by (`recommendations.md`), its
texts (`texts:`, each name a markdown file a prompt reads as `{text.<name>}`) -
and every path the definition names is relative to that directory and stays inside it, as an
action's files are relative to its own directory; two workflows never read each other's files. The
name is the folder's, the file's and the `name:` key's alike, one word, and a disagreement among the
three is refused when the file is read, so a copied directory cannot pass as the workflow it was
copied from. `init` writes one - the implementation workflow, from a request to a pull request whose
checks are green, with its agent files, prompts and schemas - and declares it in the config it
creates. Where the configuration declares `implementation`, init writes each of its files that is
missing - the whole set where the repository has no definition of it yet, and where it has one only
the shipped files that definition names, so a file taken out with its step stays out - and keeps
each one that is there, whatever it holds, saying how many it kept: an init that stopped part way is
finished by the next, and a file a repository edited is never written over. A configuration that
does not declare it gets none of it. The files a definition names are those of the tree it runs, its
uses resolved as a run resolves them (`WorkflowResolver`, a remote use left as written, for it names
no file of the repository's), and a shipped used workflow's yml the repository has not got is read
from the embedded copy init is about to write, so a pipeline taken out whole comes back whole in one
run. A file the disk will not write refuses init (13), naming the files written before it, which stay;
and where a file is missing and the repository's own definition does not read, or uses a workflow of
the repository's that does not resolve, init refuses (12, naming each problem; 13 where it cannot be
read) and writes none, since which files it names cannot be told. A file the repository's own
definition names that this tool ships elsewhere now (`WorkflowTemplates.Moved`, the item pipeline's
files an older release shipped beside the definition, read forever and never written) is not
brought back, for this build's copy is written for the new layout, and init says so in a note
naming where it ships it now; and a file of the old layout still there that the definition names no
more (`ShippedWorkflowFiles.Left`) is read by nothing, so a change a repository made to it reaches no
step, and init says so in a note naming the file read now. The shipped set is held to every rule a repository's workflow
is by this build's own tests, so a build whose own workflow does not hold fails before it ships.

A definition declares `inputs` - the values a run is started with, each with a kind, a default and
the options it takes, two whose names differ by case alone refused on every system, since a run keeps a file input's
copy in a directory of the input's name and a file system that folds case holds one for both - `params`, its own knobs
defaulted in the file and read as `param.<name>`,
and `outputs`, what the whole workflow produces, each from a step of the flow. Its steps are of
one `type` - from `orient` and `reason` through the leg steps, the fold family, the checks, git
and the forge, to `pause` - or groups holding steps of their own: a group runs its steps once for
each work item a `forEach` yields, again and again until a `repeat`'s bound is met, or once as a
block that `gathers` its members' findings into one list. A repeat that says `decideAfter` decides
at that step of each iteration, not at the iteration's end: where the step's newest visit ends
done, its `until`, its `blocking` and its bound are read there, on the iteration as it then stands
(`DecideAt`, called where the deciding step ends done and again by the schedule's walk for a session
that takes the run up from its records), and the decision is kept with that visit in the
iteration's own record (`Scope.Decision`, written through `Decide`, persisted as the step record's
`decided`), so a resume never reads it again over what has run since and a later visit of the step
in the same iteration is decided anew. The rest of that iteration starts only where the loop goes
on: a loop that asks at its bound there holds the rest of the iteration, at any depth, on its
question until the answer (`HeldByItsLoop`, the one owner of that hold, which the schedule's
drawing and `HoldOf` both read, the wait said as `FlowWaits.Answer`) - a handler its deciding
step's ending raised among it waits not started, a group one drawing none of its steps - and the
answer has it go on with the loop or end with the iteration; a loop that ends there withdraws what
of the iteration has begun no work (`EndAtTheDecision`) -
a handler its deciding step's ending raised among it, a group one made running at its raise NotRun
with all its steps (`NotRunUnbegun`) - save the steps that run after the iteration's end
(`RunsAfterItsGroup`), its always steps, which run in the always phase as a failing group's do,
waits for what is in flight and ends the loop at the iteration's end (`FinishTheDecision`), leaving
what its deciding step found, none of it acted on; at its bound, work a plan update owes the loop
has its iteration added first, as at an iteration's end; and no iteration's end re-reads a
decision made. A decision goes on past what it said in one place (`GoOnPast`), its `goesOn`
rewritten in the iteration's record: one that asked at the bound goes on once the bound allows the
next iteration - the answer `more` granted it, or work an update owes the loop had the question
withdrawn for the iteration added (`CarryWhatTheLoopsOwe`) - and one that ended the loop goes on
where an update owes it work its bound's question was never asked for, which runs again a loop that
ended at an iteration's end too (`Reopening`). The decision is written before what follows from
it, and a session that finds it with nothing of that made makes it (`Follow`, from `DecideAt` and
the iteration's end): the rest NotRun, or the bound's question asked - or, where the bound now
allows the next iteration, the loop going on - as the session that read it would have. Where the
deciding step ends any other way - skipped, failed and passed over, never run - nothing is decided
there, and the iteration's end reads them as for a loop that names no deciding step. Since the
decision is read where the deciding step ends, its `until`, `blocking` and `leftover` read of the
iteration only that step and the steps it waits for (V64), and every other step of the iteration
runs before it - one it waits for - or after it, waiting for it as a handler of its ending does
(V65), so none is left running unseen in an iteration the loop ended at its decision
(`WorkflowValidator`'s `DecisionRules`). The shipped
review loop decides at its `route`, where the review's findings are routed, so the last rework of a loop that ends at
its bound is reviewed by the round after it and what it leaves is what its last routing left - its rework and its home
audits alike. A step raised by another step's ending
says `on` - by the outcome, a failure by exit code - and sends the run back with `then`; the
schedule never starts it. Steps nest at most ten deep; every step's name is a lower-case word,
unique among its siblings and never a word a definition reads for its own. The file writes no YAML alias - a
definition writes each of its steps out, so that what it says is what it reads - and its values are read however deep
they nest, by the one YAML reader (see "Layering").

A step may be a whole workflow of its own: it says `use` - a path to the workflow's yml file,
relative to the calling workflow's directory and resolving inside the workflows folder, so a
workflow lives in a folder of its own beside the one that uses it, refused where it resolves to a
file of the workflows folder itself, holds a backslash or a part that starts or ends with a space -
the path every machine reads alike - and held to the workflows folder once links are followed by
the rule the run's own workflow is (`WorkflowValidationService.Contained`) - and `with`, the values its
inputs are filled with, each read as the input it fills declares: an expression for a `value`, a
template for a `text`, a path of the used workflow's directory for a `file`, and a single name
for a `step`, which a step of the used workflow reads as `{input.<name>}` whole in its `onFailure`
or a handler's `then`. The file a step is asked with may be read the same way (V63): one whole
input of the kind `file` naming its `prompt`, so one pipeline is asked with a different prompt by
each workflow that uses it; and a step of the used workflow may say a `when` that reads one input
of it alone, its own gate, held off where a use fills that input so - the way the shipped flow's
item pipeline holds its `redo` and `undo` off where its recovery uses it. Only where the use's
`with` value, or the input's default, is known as the file is read and makes the `when` false
(`HeldOffByItsUse`, which reads the gate as the run reads it) is such a step free of waiting for
the agent it works in and of reading a piece outside the work-item group; one the use opens runs,
and is held to both as any step is. An input the use leaves to its default is read as a `with`
value is, where the use sits, typed by the whole expression that fills it (`Yield`), as a declared
output is; a text is a template written whole; a step input read in an `onFailure` or a `then` that
the use fills with no name is refused where it is read (V62); and a policy read from an input is,
in every rule that weighs one, the policy the use around its writer fills it with
(`EffectiveOnFailure` through `PolicyFilled`) - a reasoning step under a group a use fills with
`recover` is never recovered, a use that fills it with `recover` gives the run's recovery its
failures, and `recoveryBound` is raised there. The used workflow is read as a definition of its
own and resolved into the step before anything is checked or run: its steps become the step's
members - instances named under the use as a group's are - its files are read in its own
directory, and checked there by `validate-workflow` as the run's own are (each its steps and its
recovery's steps name, its texts, the file an input of the kind `file` is filled with or defaults
to, and the advisor's and reporter's files of a use that governs itself: `WorkflowFiles.OfUse`),
and its declared outputs are the step's own once it ends (`UseOutputs`, read where the use ends
done: one that reads nothing, from a step its item skipped, is absent, and one that cannot be read
fails the use). A failure inside it that is given to a recovery reaches the nearest one declared
around the failing step, however many uses out, and else the run's own (`RecoveryReaching` walks
the scopes as the workflow declares them, `Scope.World`; `RecoveryFrom` is the one the validator's
reach and recovery-never-calls-itself rules ask), and a used workflow's recovery is held to the
run's own recovery's rules (`RecoverRules`) - its `onFailure` pause or stop - and placed and
checked however deep in other recoveries it sits.

Its `with` values are read once for each scope its steps run in - the block, each item of a
`forEach`, each iteration of a `repeat`, each raising of a handler, each item a plan update places -
by one owner (`FillUse`, reading past the use's own boundary, for the values are the caller's),
and kept in the record of the instance that scope is (the step record's `inputs`), so a resume
takes them back and never reads them again over what has run since. Every item's are read before
any item opens: a value that cannot be read fails the use, saying which input and for which item,
with nothing of it opened, and a read inside a scope whose inputs were never filled - an always
step of the failed use - is refused naming the use, never handed the caller's input of the same
name. A failure policy or a `then` read from a `step` input is filled in the scope that declares
it (`DeclaringScopeOf`) - a group's `onFailure: '{input.failTo}'` reads the input of the workflow
that declares the group, however deep the failing step - and one that reads nothing, or fills with
no policy, is said: the step's error and record say which and why, and the failure goes where the
top level sends what nothing else decides (`Unpolicied`); a handler whose `then` cannot be read
ends failed, its code `ConfigInvalid`, and its failure decides as any failure does (`ThenUnread`).
Its steps read only its inputs, its params and its own steps, never the calling run's - nor the
caller's work item, the caller's iteration before, or what raised a handler of the caller, and a
pull request's `base` inside it reads no input, for the base is filled from the run's own inputs
before any use opens (V61); every fact of the caller they need comes through an input. A visit of
a recovery stands in the scope its source failed in, but every lookup across a use's boundary -
inputs, params, texts, a failure policy, the answers - is made in the scope that declares the
recovery (`Scope.World`, which a recovery visit's scope takes from the recovery's declaring scope
and every other scope from its parent), so the run's own recovery reads the run's inputs wherever
the failure happened. A `{text.<name>}` is the nearest used workflow's own around the reading step
that declares the name, else the next one out's, else the run's (`TextsAt`, the one owner the
templates, the bar and the advisor's prompt read by).

Its budget, reporter, `pushCheckpoints` and `recommendations` are never applied, nor - unless the
use says `useParentLimits: false` - its advisor, amend, answers, limits and `codebaseGraph`, nor its
`codebaseGraph` where the run's own workflow declares one, whose shape the run's one graph then has:
the calling run's own hold, and `validate-workflow` says so beside the fingerprint of what it read,
one line for each use (`FlowUse.NotApplied`). With `useParentLimits: false` the used workflow's own
settings govern its steps key by key: a key is governed by the nearest such use around a step, by
its declaration path, that declares it - one that declares none of it governs nothing of it, so the
next one out that declares it does - and a key no such use declares stays the run's, for a use
cannot widen a run's limits by declaring nothing (`FlowUse.Governing`, the one owner of which use
governs a key, walking the root's and each use's `recover` as the definition names them, which the
engine asks through `GoverningOf` and each runner by the step's declaration path). Its
`maxReasoningAgents`, `maxParallelProcesses` and `maxOpenAgents` gate its steps as pools of their
own in the place of the run's, counted across every instance of the use (`CounterFull`); its
`maxInstances` caps the instances its steps open, across every instance of the use and in the
place of the run's own cap for them (`InstanceBoundOf`); its `maxRetries` and `backoffSeconds` are
what its steps fall back to where they say neither (`FlowUse.RetriesOf`, which `RetryCap` and the
reason runner both read, and `BackoffSecondsOf`, which the reason runner reads); its
`handoffSeconds` bounds the handoff of its paused reasoning steps; its `priority` is what its
steps' legs ask the machine's dispatch queue at, in the place of the run's (`FlowUse.PriorityOf`,
which every leg step's request reads); and its advisor recommends for
its steps' questions in the place of the run's (`SeekAdvice`): its agent and prompt files read in its own directory, its prompt handed the
inputs the use filled and the texts its steps see, its bar the workflow's own `texts.recommendations`
where it declares one (`BarOf`, reading `texts.recommendations` first, then the run's
`recommendations`, then `recommendations.md`), and each recommendation credited to the advisor that
gave it. A question of its steps is answered nearest first (`ConfiguredFor`): the step's own
answers, the groups around it within the workflow, the workflow's own `answers`, and then the use
step's own, the caller's groups and the run's. The run's one codebase graph has one shape
(`FlowUse.GraphOf`): the run's own workflow's, else the one its governing uses declare, and every
sync at a step's start or end, every serving and every graphify step of the run is made under it
(`FlowGraphSyncs.RequestOf`). Each key such a use applies is held to every rule the run's own key of
that name is (V66, `GoverningRules` calling the run's own `LimitRules`, `AdvisorKinds`,
`AnswerRules` and `GraphShapeRules`): its limits and `maxInstances` in their ranges, its advisor's
tier, model, tries and kinds, its agent definition and prompt read in its own directory and checked
against the configuration, and its keys among those the run needs, its answers to kinds its steps
raise, and its graph's patterns and languages - a use cannot declare what a run could not; and
where the run's own workflow declares no `codebaseGraph`, two such uses that shape the graph
differently are refused, for a run has one graph, of one shape. Its budget and its reporter are
carried and not applied (`FlowUse.NotApplied`): the run's budget counts its steps' spend and the
run's reporter words the run as a whole. An amend is refused where the key says false - an amend is a
run's own, and no step of a run applies one - said at validation; `preapproved` is a run's input
alone, whatever the key says. A
workflow file that uses itself, directly or through others, is refused with the circle of the
files that close it - told apart by the machine's path comparison, the calling workflow's own file
the first, so two workflows of one folder close none and a use back to the run's own file is found
at once - and steps nest at most ten deep in all, a used workflow's own counted below the step that
uses it, its recovery's as much as its flow's: the reader's own bound held across the uses of
others, so no definition that holds is deeper than the run's frozen `definition.json` can be
written. A run records each use's resolution - the called workflow's name and its fingerprint, for
a local one the digest of its parsed definition taken as the run's own definition's is, so a
comment or line endings change nothing, and for a remote one, or one inside it, its commit - in the
definition it freezes, and a resume is refused where what the called workflow brings the run changed
since the run began - its steps, inputs, params, outputs and recovery, the settings of its own it
carries, its texts and the keys it declares unapplied, compared with the rest of the definition as
the run's own steps are (`FlowResume.Said`); the fingerprint is left out of that, for a local one's is
a digest the build that began the run made, which no frozen definition holds to make again, and a
remote one's commit is in its name. The shipped implementation workflow uses the
mechanism for itself: its item pipeline - written once in `item-pipeline/item-pipeline.yml` - is
used by its rounds (`implementPrompt: prompts/implement.md`, `alternatives: 'true'`,
`failTo: recover`) and by its recovery (`prompts/remedy.md`, `alternatives: 'false'`,
`failTo: pause`, for the recovery cannot call itself) alike, and the validator and the tests count
the resolved tree, every step of every use a step as a group's are.

A use may name a workflow beyond the repository: `owner/repo/path/workflow.yml@ref`, as GitHub
Actions spells `uses` - a repository's name may be dotted, as an organisation's `.github` is - or
the same under a GitHub Enterprise host the configuration names. The ref is held to git's own rules
for a ref's name (`WorkflowRemote.RefProblem`, before anything is asked) and resolved at the run's
start through git itself (`WorkflowRemoteFetcher` over `WorkflowGitFetch`, git run in a directory
of the fetch's own, so no configuration of the calling tree's decides what is fetched or who it is
fetched as) and the repository's own refs, every branch and tag listed whole in one call
(`git ls-remote --tags --heads`): its tag, an annotated tag's tag object peeled through each tag
object it names - however many, the ones peeled kept (`Chain`), so a chain that closes on itself
is refused where it closes - to the commit, or, where the pin is `any`, its branch. A repository
git answers is not there, or that the credential cannot see, is named as that. The repository is
fetched as a partial clone of commits and tag objects alone (`WorkflowClone`, `--filter=tree:0`):
the one ref a tag or a branch names, at its tip (`--depth=1`), what the clone fetched being what
is read and recorded; or, for a commit named by its SHA, or recorded by a run and no longer
cached, every branch and tag with their history, the commit proved the repository's own by git's
own walk over every ref (`for-each-ref --contains`): GitHub serves a commit of any fork under the
repository's own name (the imposter commit), and one no branch or tag reaches is refused. The
commit's tree is then asked for by its id with no blob (`fetch --stdin --filter=blob:none`) and
read whole at the workflow's directory (`ls-tree -r -t`); a symbolic link, a submodule, a path
rooted on any platform or holding `..`, `\`, `:` or a control character, two paths one where case
is folded (`WorkflowCache.TreePathProblems`), or a file the use names that the directory does not
hold refuses the whole before a blob is fetched. Every blob of the directory is asked for by its
id in one transfer, nothing checked out - so no attribute of the remote's own runs a filter - read
as git stores it and checked against the hash the tree gives of it (git's own blob hash, SHA-1 of
`blob <size>\0` and the bytes), of any number of files and any size, each transfer told every five
minutes while it lasts, and nothing is cached where a check fails; any answer that does not read
is git's failure, named, never an exception of the runtime's. What
is cached lives in `workflow-cache/` under this user's own directory for this tool
(`UserState.Directory`, the root every per-user file of the tool lives under), named the first time
the cache is used so a process with no home of its own still runs every workflow that names nothing
remote: each blob as the bytes the forge gave at `blobs/<first 2 hex>/<remaining 38 hex>` - decoded
only where text is read, a byte order mark dropped as a repository's own file read drops it - one
entry per repository, commit and directory at `entries/<sha256 of the parts>.json`, and each ref's
newest resolution at `resolutions/<sha256 of the parts>.json`, each read strictly as every state file
is (`JsonStateFile`) and an entry held to the key it was looked up by, its commit and blobs 40 hex
characters and its paths the tree's rule's. Every file of an entry is hashed again as it is read, so
a blob changed on disk is refused and its directory fetched again. One machine-wide lock
(`MachineWideFile`) orders what a pruning decides against what a fetch and a use record, and it is
held for one record, or one batch of a pruning's removals (`WorkflowCache.BlobsPerHold`), at a time -
never across a fetch's blobs or a whole pruning, so another process waits for it a moment, and a
wait that lasts is told every five minutes while its holder lives: a blob is named by its content, so it is written outside the lock before its entry, and
the entry is written under it only once every blob it names is there, written again where a pruning
took it meanwhile (`WorkflowCache.Write`); a pruning reads under the lock which blobs the entries hold
before it removes one, and reads each stale entry again under it before removing it, so a use since
keeps it; and a use is recorded under the lock with the look that its entry is still there
(`WorkflowCache.Hold`), so an entry a pruning removed as it was read is fetched again, never answered
as held. A second run of a pinned SHA reads the cache with no network, and
a tag needs one call at each run's start; a run records each use's resolution - the remote commit SHA
stands in the fingerprint a local workflow's parsed digest holds - and `FlowService` hands the frozen definition, with
the run's own copy of its remote workflows, to the check a resume goes through, so each remote use resolves to the commit the run began with and
never resolves again: a tag or branch that moved since changes no run already started, and only a
change to what a local file says refuses it as before. A resolution carries every file of its
directory as it fetched or read and hashed it (`WorkflowRemoteResolution.Files`), and nothing after
it reads the cache again: the check reads a remote workflow's files, a use inside it and its schemas
from there, `export-workflow --from` writes them from there, and a run keeps them beside its frozen
definition, in the cache's own shape under its directory (`OrchestratorLayout.RemoteWorkflowsDirectory`,
`WorkflowCache.OfRun`), filled at each session's start from the check that let the session begin
(`WorkflowCache.Keep`, which keeps again only what the copy does not hold whole), and read by its steps
as they run (`WorkflowNamedFiles.OfRun`). A run's files are frozen rather than its entries held against
a pruning because freezing makes what a run reads the run's own, as its definition already is: a
pruning then decides by nothing but the cache's own records, never by a guess at which runs are live
and which of them hold which entry - a run whose engine died, or one resumed on another day, would
otherwise hold its entries forever or lose them - and a resume, which resolves each use to the commit
it began with again, reads it from the run's own copy first (`WorkflowRecordedUse`, which
`WorkflowRunRecord` hands the fetcher from the check), proved the repository's own, read and hashed
when the run began, then from the user's cache, and from the forge - proved again as any commit named
by its SHA is - only where neither holds it whole: one order of where a recorded resolution's files
come from, whoever runs the command, so the check a session goes through reads the very bytes its
steps read, and neither a pruning of the cache, the network not being there, nor a tag deleted or a
branch pushed over since refuses a run that started; and the session keeps again only what the run's
copy does not hold whole.
Trust is a person's decision, never a response's: a remote workflow directs agents and machine
steps in the calling repository, so `workflowSources` in
`config.json` allows its owner (`allow`, empty by default); names each GitHub Enterprise host with its
one credential (`hosts.<host>.credential`, `{"from": "env", "name": "<VARIABLE>"}`, required), handed
to git in its environment - every helper git's configuration names cleared, and one that answers
with it alone put in their place (`GitCredentialValues`), so no command line carries it - and
written nowhere else, a host with none, or whose variable is not
set, refused before it is asked anything, while a github.com call keeps the helpers git's
configuration names, the machine's own `gh` login
and is given no enterprise token; pins the refs it takes (`pin`: `tag-or-commit` by default, `commit`,
or `any`, which allows a branch, warned of wherever one is resolved); and says what stands in where
the network keeps the forge from being reached (`offline`: `refuse`, or `last-resolved`, the cache's
newest resolution of the ref, warned of where it stands in). A resolution the cache stands in with,
offline or under an agent, is held to the pin by one rule (`WorkflowRemoteFetcher.CachedResolution`):
a ref the cache last resolved as a branch is refused where the pin is not `any`, as the forge's own
answer would be. Only a call that never reached the forge -
git's own words for a name that did not resolve, or a connection that was refused or never made
(`WorkflowGitFetch.Unreached`) - is the network not being there; a forge that answered, refusing the
credential or naming a repository or ref that is not there, is refused with what git said, and
nothing stands in for it. A remote workflow's own name inside the run is its cache place,
`remote/<host>/<owner>/<repo>/<commit>/<dir>`: its files resolve against its entry as a local
workflow's do against its directory - through the same `WorkflowNamedFiles` rule, the reader routing
the reserved `remote/` place to the cache - a relative use inside it resolves inside the same entry
(`WorkflowResolution.ReadCached`, the resolution carrying the remote one's place down, a use that
leaves the fetched directory refused), named under `remote/` by its own directory and read at run
time from the entry of the nearest directory above it that the cache holds at that commit
(`WorkflowCache.FindNamed`); no local use resolves under `remote/`, the cache's own reserved place in
the workflows folder, and no workflow is named `remote` (`WorkflowName`). A remote workflow's schemas
are held to the subset of JSON Schema the engine reads by the one rule a local one's are
(`WorkflowFiles.SchemaProblems`), read from what its resolution read. A fetch refused for what the
source is (`WorkflowResolution.RefusesTheSource`: 13, or 12 for a workflow file that is no text) - not
allowed, a host or credential not named, a ref the pin refuses or that is not the repository's own,
a file the directory does not hold, a forge that answered and refused - is the definition's problem,
said with the use, so `validate-workflow` ends 12 and a run is not started. A fetch that could not run
is none, and goes on with its own code: the forge not reached with nothing standing
in - `offline: refuse`, or `last-resolved` with no whole resolution of the ref cached - as the call
that did not reach it raised it (20); git failing otherwise, or answering what does not read (20);
and the workflow cache that could not be
named, written or read, or whose lock could not be taken, which every failure of
the cache's own ends with (`WorkflowCache.FailedExit`, 21) - `workflow-cache list` and `prune` among
them. `validate-workflow`, `run-orchestrator` and a resume end with that code, the line they end on
naming the workflow cache. A command that runs under an agent never reaches the forge nor writes the
cache: the fetcher tells it by the one rule `run-side-task` refuses itself by
(`AgentAncestry.UnderAnAgentAsync`) - the agent's mark (`DSSHARNESS_UNDER_AGENT`), or a process of this
tool's above it in the process tree, which no form of taking the mark away reaches, one whose tree
cannot be read taken as no person's - and resolves from the cache alone - a ref by its newest
resolution the pin takes - writing nothing, not even the use's date, and refuses what the cache does
not hold whole saying what made the command an agent's and where a person fills the cache instead, in
the one wording `run-side-task`'s refusal gives too (`AgentAncestryAnswer.Why`: the mark, the process
of this tool's by its name and id, or why the tree could not be read; `AgentAncestryAnswer.APersonsShell`:
a shell of the person's own, which no process of this tool's started and which carries no mark, where
`dssharness validate-workflow` or `dssharness export-workflow --from` fetches it), so a person told no
is never sent to run again the command that was refused; a record or a blob of the cache's that could
not be read is the cache's own failure there as everywhere nothing is fetched over it (21), never a
workflow the cache does not hold (`WorkflowCache.ReadBytes`: a blob gone or changed on disk leaves its
entry not whole, one that could not be read is the cache's failure). So `validate-workflow` and
`export-workflow` stay among the verbs open to an agent (`AgentPolicy.OpenVerbs`). The rule takes a
command any process of this tool's starts for an agent's - a leg's, a check's or a machine step's as
much as an agent's own - because the process tree is the one fact an agent's child cannot change, and
no process of the tool's says which of its children are an agent's: a record the engine kept of its
own processes - a file, or a word of the environment - an agent's command could take away wherever no
isolation holds it, as it can the mark, and a list of the verbs that start agents would be a second
hand-kept rule beside the code that starts them. The refusal says so, naming the process, rather than
the rule being narrowed.
`validate-workflow` names the workflow cache's directory on the line it ends on wherever it went to
resolve a remote use, whether the workflows hold or not, and in `--json` (`cache`) on every exit; a
stop of it that came of a fetch names it in its line too.
`export-workflow --from <use> --to <dir>` vendors a remote workflow at its resolved commit - every
file of its directory and `source.md`, a note of where it came from and how the commit came about
where that is worth a word (the cache's last resolution standing in, or a branch), a directory
holding a `source.md` of its own refused (13); a workflow name or `--shipped` beside `--from`, or a
`--from` that names no remote workflow (`WorkflowRemote.Source` answers none for a blank one), is a
usage error (10), and the folder is looked at before anything is fetched, so one that is there is
refused (13) with nothing written anywhere; its line names the workflow cache it fetched into, a
refusal after the fetch says what it fetched is kept there, and its `--json` names the cache
(`cache`) for every export but the shipped one's - so a team can review what is written and use it
as `./`; the `workflow-cache` verb lists the cache's entries and the files of its
own it could not read, and prunes, by the days an entry went unused and unfetched (`--unused-days`,
required, 0 or more - any number, those reaching back past the clock's start putting the cut-off
there), the entries, the resolutions that named them and the blobs no entry left
holds - keeping every blob an entry it keeps holds (`WorkflowCache.BlobOf`, the inverse of the blob's
path), removing no blob while a file of the cache's own could not be read, and ending incomplete (21)
